speechtext:
I have the honour of laying on the table of the House the Seventeenth Annual Report of the Commissioner of Official Languages for calendar year 1987, pursuant to Section 34(1) of the Official Languages Act.

I would remind Hon. Members that this document stands referred to a Standing Joint Committee on Official Languages.

Mr. Speaker, it is my honour, indeed, it is a pleasure to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 from petitioners who are concerned that the federal Government lacks a mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade deal with the United States.
They believe that the trade deal negotiated by the Government threatens the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty since it removes the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control foreign ownership and to develop Canadian energy resources in the best interests of Canadians. It certainly does not equalize the opportunities between the regions of the country.
For a whole set of other reasons they are calling upon Parliament to dissolve now to give the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade deal during a national general election.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: OPPPOSITION TO THE EXPULSION OF TURKISH NATIONALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege for me to table a number of petitions in accordance with Standing Order 106. The petitions of the undersigned residents of Canada read as follows: Your petitioners humbly state that considering the decision of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to proceed as of March 20, 1988, with the deportation of 2,000 Turkish nationals, men, women and children; considering the particular circumstances that led these people to come to Canada and the dramatic consequences their return to Turkey would have for these people; considering the legitimacy of granting them, on compassionate grounds, the right to settle in Canada; wherefore your petitioners humbly pray Parliament to ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration to reconsider his decision.
[DOT] (mo)

Mr. Speaker, I have the duty of presenting a petition from constituents of mine. It is an honour to do this on behalf of persons resident in northern communities in my riding along the Canadian National Railway line through Armstrong and, particularly, in Mud River.
These constituents protest, along with so many other of my constituents, that the Conservative Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised in the course of the bilateral trade negotiations that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised. In fact, the proposed trade agreement would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and undermine our ability to build a society distinct from that of the U.S.
The agreement denies just that, secure access to the U.S. market which the Government promised. It threatens hundreds of thousands of Canadians and their jobs.
These Canadians protest and ask the Parliament of Canada take note of these realities and dangers, that it dissolve and give the people of Canada an opportunity to decide what they think of this trade deal with the United States.

subsubtopic: IMMIGRATION-REQUEST THAT THE TURKS BE ALLOWED TO REMAIN ON HUMANITARIAN GROUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak for many of my constituents and other Montrealers who are extremely fair-minded and who wish to speak to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to ask him to prevent and not to expel the 2,000 Turkish men, women and children who are here because they were unaware of Canadian law. They were misled and given inaccurate information by unscrupulous travel agents and advertisements in their papers in their own areas.
These people are innocent victims. The error is on the part of the Government which knew in the fall of 1986 what the situation was and took no action to stem the tide.
Because of the particular circumstances, they ask that these people be allowed to stay on humanitarian grounds.
I deposit a petition with 25 names on it coming from Plamondon, Mountain Sights, Barclay, Letourneux, and the area of Marquette and Desrosiers Streets, in Montreal.
I have an additional petition with 18 names on it. These people feel the same way. They live on Cote-des-Neiges, Hudson, Queen Mary, in Laval, in the Town of Mount Royal, on Saint-Denis-in fact, across the spectrum of the large City of Montreal.
The last petition I would like to deposit-

-reads as follows:
That considering the decision of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to proceed as of March 10, 1988, with the deportation of 2,000 Turkish nationals, men, women and children; considering the particular circumstances that led these people to come to Canada and the dramatic consequences their return to Turkey would have for these people; considering the legitimacy of granting them, on compassionate grounds, the right to settle in Canada; wherefore your petitioners humbly pray Parliament to ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration to reconsider his decision.
These petitions come from Jean-Rivard, Chabot, Laval, Garneau, Berri and other streets.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have a number of petitions signed by residents of the Montreal area which concern the 2,000 Turkish men, women and children whom the Minister of Employment and Immigration is threatening with deportation.
Mr. Speaker, the undersigned refer to the innocence of these people. They were victims of misleading advertising. They were not aware that their arrival in Canada was not in accordance with Canadian procedures. These are people in need who sold everything they had to pay for their ticket to Canada.
The undersigned also stress the responsibility of the Government, since it became aware of the situation in the fall of 1986 but took five or six months to react.
Therefore, your petitioners ask Parliament to ask the Minister of Employment and Immigration to reconsider his decision. The law must be interpreted justly and fairly, and that is what your petitioners are asking.
I have two petitions, each signed by forty-four people from Sherbrooke Street in Montreal, from Mountain Sights Street, Boulevard l'Acadie, Cote-des-Neiges, Fullum Street in Montreal East, Pointe-aux-Trembles, Henri-Bourassa Street, by people from Stanstead who signed these petitions, from Bourbonniere Street in Montreal and Cote-Saint-Luc.
Today we tabled petitions with about 400 signatures. More petitions are being signed in Montreal, and these will be tabled as we receive them over the next few days.

The House resumed from March 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crombie that Bill C-93, an Act for the preservation and enhancement of multiculturalism in Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On debate, the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges).
Mr. Speaker, I had finished my time for debate. I believe there is now a 10-minute period for questions and comments.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On questions and comments the Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Fine-stone).

The Chairman of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism is to be complimented for the very careful exercise and leadership which he demonstrated as chairman of that committee. He proposed a very comprehensive list of recommendations which I read with a great deal of interest over the weekend. I would like to ask the chairman how he now feels about press clippings which indicate that the multiculturalism Bill received a cool welcome, that it is an empty promise on multiculturalism, it will not stem the rivalries, it is strictly une loi plus declaratoire qu'executoire.
The chairman called for at least the creation of a Minister and a commissioner of multiculturalism to watch over the application of the law. With the present structure the Minister watches himself and answers to himself. There is a less than enthusiastic response from the one-third of Canadians whom this Bill is supposed to enable to realize their full equality in our society. How does the Hon. Member respond to that? How can the Hon. Member stand in his place and compliment the Minister and be satisfied with the present Bill? Is the Hon. Member not hoping for changes when it goes to legislative committee, and does the Hon. Member plan to be at the legislative committee?

In answer to the questions asked by my hon. friend, the response to the multiculturalism Bill, building the Canadian mosaic, was very positive. We had a very good response.
The Hon. Member asked the question about why we have not appointed a Minister or a commissioner of multiculturalism. I grant that those are two areas in which we as a committee were in agreement. As I stated in my speech, I have been

March 22, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
around this place long enough to know that one does not get everything one wants at the start. We have our foot in the door, and a very substantive foot in the door of the department of multiculturalism. Hopefully, it will open the door in the future for a commissioner and also a full Minister. I am still hopeful that many of our recommendations will be accepted over a period of time. But, as I say, I have been here long enough to know that we will not get everything we want the first time, but I am hoping.

One week ago I listened with interest when the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) spoke on Bill C-93, a very important piece of legislation. He said some very interesting things. I wish to commend him for raising the issue of group rights in his speech, and ask if he would be able to say something more on that subject. I ask that particularly in the context of what the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) suggests, for all the good things that one can say about Bill C-93, it is half of a good Bill. There is no machinery here. The provision for a commissioner, and provision for strong action by the Government has not been provided. It institutionalizes the status quo. We all recognize that the Canadian status quo involves very little respect for group rights.
The most massive failure to deal humanely and imaginatively with group rights is to be found in the failure of First Ministers' conferences to place the aboriginal right of selfgovernment into the Constitution, and the failure of the Department of Indian Affairs to lead or to work energetically with aboriginal peoples in establishing how they will govern themselves and how they will develop their group rights in Canada.
Together with my colleagues on the committee, I appreciate the careful leadership given by the Hon. Member for Grey- Simcoe. I appreciate the optimism that he still feels after all these years in Parliament. I particularly appreciated his expression of optimism that the Bill would be amended.
I would ask him to say a little on the establishment of group rights, recognition of those rights in a society that is all too attuned to individual rights and all too rarely aware of the importance of recognizing groups in Canada and providing for them. I particularly ask him in what way we might establish institutions, and I encourage him to suggest what he would like to see added to the second half of the Bill. The problem is that we in opposition cannot amend the Bill. We can amend it in the detail that is there, but we can hardly add substantive sections.
It is necessary for the Hon. Member to respond to what I know is the pressure from the ethnocultural communities across Canada and from the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, for the Government to recognize the lacuna that is represented by the second half of the Bill, or what simply is not there, and to fill that with substantial legislation.
The original Official Languages Act established a Commissioner of Official Languages. The revised Bill which the legislative committee begins considering this afternoon does not need to add to it. The Official Languages Act of 1969 established that commissioner's office, and now the multiculturalism Bill does not do that.
Would the Hon. Member offer us some more insight into group rights, and his thoughts on the Government taking up the challenge and giving us the second half of what could be a really good Bill, if only the Government acted on that.

I thank my hon. friend and committee member for the question. As far as I am concerned, we are officially a bilingual and multicultural country, and to me that means that everyone in Canada should be treated equally under every circumstance whatever his or her background, whether it is European or Asiatic. Everyone in Canada should treat everyone else the way they expect to be treated themselves.
I look forward to the day when we will not require a multiculturalism committee or multiculturalism department because everyone will be tuned into the multiculturalism aspect of Canada. This will affect all the groups in Canada. There are something like 102 different ethnocultural groups in Canada today.
As far as the Bill is concerned, I would certainly like to see amendments. If I am chosen to sit on that legislative committee, I will be proposing legislation to change any aspect of the Bill that would actually further the cause of multiculturalism. I am looking forward to working with my hon. friend on that committee, together with the rest of the members of the committee, and see what we come up with.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to address this very important Canadian policy of multiculturalism and to speak on Bill C-93. All Canadians are very proud of our particular unique tradition of multiculturalism. In Canada we often refer to the fact that we are not a melting pot as in the United States. We have so many people who come from different lands who have brought such rich culture and experience with them. We recognize this and have made it a part of our own Canadian mosaic.
It is important that we have a multiculturalism Bill. This is the second such Bill. It is a little stronger than the one presented by the Liberals, but it still needs to be strengthened in many ways. I will speak to that in a moment.
The first part of the Bill recognizes the main principles based on many statutes, the Charter of Rights, and our international covenants which commit us to recognizing the rights of all people and all cultural groups. Interestingly, the Bill also refers to aboriginal people who have constitutional rights. I wonder how those same aboriginal people and their leaders will feel. I think that they may have some reservations about being grouped under multiculturalism. Certainly, most native people whom I talk to, and I agree, feel that they have very unique rights and must be dealt with separately. They
March 22, 1988

have much to contribute to Canada and are contributing much from their unique cultures.
The Bill is based upon the premise that we are a bilingual country and that the larger community of Canada is comprised of many cultural communities. I note that the principles are not spelled out in the same way as they were recommended by the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism. Perhaps in themselves they need to be strengthened, but unfortunately this is not something we can do at this stage.
For the purpose of comparison I should like to refer to the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism dated June, 1987. Its first recommendation was that the new multiculturalism policy should embody the following eight principles: multiculturalism for all Canadians, advancement of multiculturalism within a bilingual framework, equality of opportunity, preservation and enhancement of cultural diversity, elimination of discrimination, establishment of affirmative measures, enhancement of heritage languages, and support for immigrant integration. I am sorry that these particular principles were not repeated in this very important Bill.
It is important that we start with basic principles. However, principles are just lip service and window dressing unless we provide the mechanisms to achieve the goals. This is the area in which the Bill is weak. Critics from a whole range of ethnic organizations have expressed concern in this regard as well.
As our spokesperson in this area has said, there is no new means of achieving a genuine multicultural Canada as recommended by the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism. In effect the Bill is a symbolic gesture, and we need something more than that.
The Bill should have provided for a department of multiculturalism. It should have provided for a commissioner of multiculturalism. Also, there should have been provision for a research centre on multiculturalism and, I would say, on multiculturalism and racism. The Standing Committee on Multiculturalism and a number of other groups have criticized the Bill for these reasons.
At this point I should like to commend particularly the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) for his very outstanding work in the field of multiculturalism. I was very impressed with the document he prepared in June, 1987 entitled "A Living Diversity, Multiculturalism for All". It was a very excellent document on the aspects of multiculturalism which we feel are very important and which we stress very strongly. For example, too often the whole aspect of racism is left out when we talk about multiculturalism.
Manitoba has established a structure which deals with some of the problems. Its Government established the Manitoba Intercultural Council to meet with Ministers to press for action. That is what we do not have here. We do not have a
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
structure, a commissioner, or representatives from the multicultural community who really have a recognized official role in advocating and pressing for changes.
Just to compare the kinds of structures with which I am familiar, the only multicultural representative in British Columbia is one person who acts as a multicultural goodwill ambassador and attends multicultural events. Well, it is very nice, in a pleasant way, to attend events, but we need something to deal with problems and issues. We have that in the City of Vancouver. It is known as the Race Relations Committee and is very involved. These kinds of structures are very important.
It is too bad the Bill does not provide the teeth to allow for major criticism of government policies and to look at the problems of multicultural communities.
The Canadian Ethnocultural Council has put out a very excellent document making several recommendations for improvement. I should just like to refer to it very quickly. It suggests that Bill C-93 should have included a commissioner to monitor the implementation of the Act, that there should have been various amendments to the wording of the Act, toughening it up with words like "shall" rather than "should" to express the Government's commitment to multiculturalism, and that federal-provincial co-operation should be spelled out, along with official involvement of the provinces.
The Minister's advisory committee should be appointed on the recommendation of the multicultural communities. Similarly, there should be more equitable participation of minority individuals in the form of increased appointments from the grass roots communities, not just from the elite here in Ottawa.
The council also mentioned three very important areas which were unfortunately omitted from the Bill; the multicultural department, the need for increased multicultural funding, and the need for charitable tax status for ethnocultural organizations to allow them to increase their own fund raising abilities. I think these matters are extremely important.
I should like to very quickly mention two statements in the "Social Infopac", a document prepared by the Social Planning Council of Metropolitan Toronto. It indicates that multicultural policies at the federal and provincial levels have been in place for decades but that the rhetoric of multiculturalism seems to have outstripped the achievements of policies. The Bill tends to be heavy on rhetoric and weak on ways of implementing that rhetoric. It goes on to indicate that multiculturalism is a commitment to a pluralistic society. It proposes that we not only tolerate and respect differences but acknowledge the need to reduce disparities and barriers which prohibit diverse cultural and racial groups from participating effectively as citizens.
Particularly, I should like to concentrate on the fact that too often we think of multiculturalism as a collage of very colourful events. I am sure that we all enjoy many ethnic

March 22, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
events in our ridings. My riding of Vancouver East is a wonderful place. I think it is the outstanding multicultural community of Canada. There are constant events to celebrate the Chinese New Year, Italian carnivals, and the Japanese Summer Festival in the heartland of the Japanese community. We visit Sikh temples where we experience their events, food, and so on. Of course there are many events in the native communities such as those in the longhouse. July 1 is a mosaic of many different kinds of events in our community. I think particularly of the events at Britannia Centre in my riding, a multicultural service centre of schools, recreational facilities, and a library. Such events are wonderful. They are the joy of multiculturalism. However, they are not enough.
Our government policies and programs must take positive steps to ensure that persons of all ethnic backgrounds have equal rights and equal opportunities and that they do not experience racism. We must face up to the fact that racism and lack of opportunities are very prevalent, particularly with people of colour in society today. I attended a number of meetings of the Immigrant and Visible Women's Council which was formed in a conference last year. We heard over and over again the kind of double discrimination that women of colour face. I am sure men feel the same way.
Government policy must open jobs to visible minorities in a much more direct way with stronger affirmative action programs. I have heard many people comment recently that on TV news broadcasts we have many more visible minority commentators, guests and so on. Soon this situation will be taken for granted and we will not have to speak about it. But are persons of colour, visible minorities if you like, moving up in the public service and in other kinds of jobs? Perhaps they are getting in the door through employment equity but we have yet to find out. This is the first year we will be getting reports about it. Are persons of colour moving up into all levels of our public service? I suspect not, according to what I was told by the women's conference.
We must take tangible steps to protest racism and to uphold our Charter by acknowledging past injustices. This is why redress of the injustices that Canadians of Japanese origin experienced must be made. Chinese immigrants who came here at the turn of the century experienced injustice, but in a different way. They were not yet citizens of Canada. The Chinese and Japanese cultural groups and their wide group of supporters now say that we must wipe out these injustices from our history and our consciences. It is appalling that, after election promises to do something, there have been only two or three series of negotiations with Canadians of Japanese origin who lost their properties, were displaced, lost their communities and dignity as a result of injustices during World War II. It is appalling that the Government will not compensate them.
There was a big meeting recently in my riding on this matter. Not just one ethnic group is concerned about the matter. There are coalitions building and Canadians from all
backgrounds want us to take a stand. Individuals who are now elderly must have fair redress for their losses. Why shouldn't they? The Americans have done something in the U.S.A.. It is a shame that our Government refuses to do anything, to negotiate fairly with the organizations who represent the Japanese Canadians. We want the issue settled once and for all; wiped from our consciences and our history books. We want our children to be proud that we have recognized these people.
Similarly, I have spoken many times in this House about the Chinese head tax. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised to meet with Canadians of Chinese origin to acknowledge the imposed injustice, not only by the head tax laws early in the century but as well by the Chinese Exclusion Act which for many years prohibited Canadian citizens of Chinese origin from bringing their wives and families over from China. Here again the Prime Minister promised that his Government would meet with people and settle this issue. Now the Cabinet has instructed the Minister responsible for Multiculturalism that he cannot even meet with the Chinese Canadian National Council. How can you begin to discuss issues if you are not able to meet with the people concerned? I am honoured to be on an all-Party committee that has met once with the Chinese Canadian National Council. We are hamstrung unless the Government is prepared to act.
What about the many injustices and the stigma which is being stirred up by recent events, and I am thinking of the Sikh community. There were incidents last summer involving Sikhs who were refugee claimants at the time. We heard inflammatory language and the policies of the Government stimulated racism. In my riding, and in many others, we had numerous calls from people who expressed overt racism toward this group. Although no one condones terrorism, I do not think the statements by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) have helped multicultural relations in recent days through his boycott of certain Sikh organizations. This is overt discrimination, but there are subtle discriminations as well.
I want to mention StatsCanada. I get so irritated when I look at the format for collecting information, which has for years focused primarily on groups from Europe. It is as if Asia and the people who came to Canada from there did not exist. Only recently have a few countries been noted as countries of origin. So we do not have recognition in the data on people who for many years have come from Asian countries to provide leadership in Canada.
I mentioned double discrimination faced by immigrant women, but there is triple discrimination as well. Not only are they faced with discrimination because they are immigrants and women, but also because many of them are coloured. We must have many more positive programs to assist women and to open opportunities; for instance, English as a second language, many community support programs, more relevant employment training and child care in relation to all programs. We must entrench our multicultural heritage in the Constitution; that is what we heard from multicultural and ethnic
March 22, 1988

groups when debating the Meech Lake Accord. There was concern that the rights of the minorities were not made specific at that time.
On September 3 last year I raised this problem in the House through a petition from Mosaic which is a multicultural group in my riding. The Canadian Ethnic Cultural Council also states that Section 15 of the Charter should define freedom from discrimination based on multicultural factors by adding "race, national or ethnic origin, colour (or) religion".
There are many things we must do. There are many omissions from the Bill. Basically it is a good start. I am sure that in committee there will be many amendments to the Bill. I was pleased to hear the previous speaker say that he will be assisting in this regard. Let us make it a very effective Bill and let us make sure that we remove racism from Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened again with interest to the words of the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). She spoke from her own experience in her constituency and her experience of life on the West Coast, a part of Canada where Asian migration to Canada is important. There is the establishment of communities of people from Japan, China and other parts of Asia as well as from the dominion of India in its day and from neighbouring countries. People have come to Canada from various places to find homes here. I appreciate her emphasis on the importance of legislation that will ensure respect for the rights of all communities in Canada to be enhanced by the Canadian Government.
I want to explore a related aspect in the Government's interaction with communities and representatives from the communities. I have a question of her about the possibility of a model. In fact, something like the Advisory Council on the Status of Women might be taken up by the Government to advance the cause of multiculturalism. Let me explain what I am thinking of here by picking up on the Hon. Member's observations about the Manitoba Intercultural Council. It is a very important body, as she suggested.
During a western multicultural tour almost exactly a year ago, I had the privilege of being in Winnipeg and being able to sit in on a joint meeting of the executive of the Manitoba Intercultural Council and a good part of the provincial Cabinet. I was impressed first by the fact that the premier, the Minister of Finance who had previously been the Minister responsible for multicultural matters and the Minister of Education of the Province of Manitoba were there, quite a diversity of Ministers over and above the Minister for Culture, Heritage and Recreation, who of course is primarily responsible. They were all gathered at the table to consider an agenda of important concerns which the Manitoba Intercultural Council had put forward.
This is a council formed largely of representatives chosen by the communities under legislation which the New Democratic
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Government put forward to ensure that the council would be genuinely representative and would articulate the concerns of the communities. We have not had anything remotely resembling that in multiculturalism federally. We have had behind closed doors advisory councils to a succession of Ministers. The Bill intends to perpetuate that particular model. It is greatly to be regretted that that is the model the Government plans to continue with, since it is not prepared to do anything on the matter of the commissioner or on a strong ministry.
I wonder if the Hon. Member, from her intense involvement in the women's cause and her advancement of that cause on the federal scene, would have any thoughts about how the model provided by the Advisory Council on the Status of Women might conceivably provide a federal example of a multicultural body. Such a body would be publicly established, speaking publicly, doing research and able to press the Government openly and gather support for the endeavours of others outside Government. What possibilities are there for drawing on one model and applying it to the multicultural area?

Mr. Speaker, I think that was the expert speaking, but he has raised a very interesting point. There are some great advantages in having advisory councils, but if there were to be something outside Government, I would hope that it would use a different way of appointing people than is used in the traditional government bodies we have now, like the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, although it is doing very good work and has an excellent director. I have always advocated that there should be some way for women's communities across Canada to nominate people for that body and that they not just be political appointees. I do not think we need that kind of tokenism in a new body.
We should also keep in mind that when it comes to women's issues, there is a government Department, Status of Women Canada, although there is not a commissioner. Perhaps it would be a very good idea to have one. There needs to be a mechanism both within Government and without to press for the policies.

Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks I alluded to the matter of racism in Canada and to the need for action along those lines. I wonder if the Hon. Member for Vancouver East could say something about the matter of the strong action that is required from her experience in the Province of British Columbia and, of course, in national politics.
The New Democratic commitment to equality, the necessity for doing more than just talking about fine principles and actually advancing those appeared in the debate on Bill C-62, the employment equity Bill. There we had a situation that is all too similar to this one. It was a Bill that enunciated some fine principles and did provide for some reporting, but it was only under extreme pressure that the Government responded in any way at all to the need for something more than the

March 22, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
gathering of information, something more than a vague setting of goals for advancement.
I have been profoundly distressed by the resemblance of Bill C-93 to Bill C-62. It states the principles and puts up the window-dressing but does not provide the kind of machinery that is required. We have a Bill that relates to the concerns of various groups, including the concerns of women of all colours and of all backgrounds, recognizing that women of colour, immigrant and visible-minority women particularly face great impediments to their advancement in Canadian society.
The similarity of Bill C-93 to Bill C-62 concerns me a great deal, and I wonder whether the Hon. Member could expand on the importance of having strong legislation. Perhaps she could express her thoughts about the possibility of the Government providing such legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I think I said in my remarks that to deal with racism is probably the most important area for policy and action on the part of the Government. Groups are quite capable of dealing with community events and multiculturalism as it exists now, but we must face the question of racism head on.
The Hon. Member is more of an expert on the Bill itself than am I, but as we deal with amendments to it we will look at how to strengthen it. Certainly there does not appear to be the kind of mechanism in it to deal with that issue.
I think it is also very important that we as a society look at the prevention of racism. I know that some committees at the community level are looking at how to do more in schools with language and with books to show that we have a multicultural society and to discuss these issues. As I mentioned, children should know about incidents of discrimination in our history, and they should know that under our Charter those kinds of incidents would no longer be tolerated.

Mr. Speaker, as the Member for a portion of a city which can justly claim to be the birthplace of multiculturalism in Canada, I take great pride in the privilege of being able to intervene in today's debate.
Before dwelling on the merits of the Bill before us, I think I should say something about an honour which on May 6 will be conveyed to three residents of my constituency to be made Members of the Order of Canada on that date at a ceremony in Rideau Hall. What is remarkable is that no one has referred to the fact that each of the three of them represents what we celebrate here today, our multicultural heritage.
Mr. Krishan Joshee, who has lived in this country for approximately 30 years, was a distinguished educator and is now a public administrator. He was born in India, taught in Ethiopia, latterly in remote northern Alberta and most recently in the City of Edmonton, rising to the position of vice principal of one of Edmonton's Catholic schools, a remarkable achievement for a man of the Hindu religion. He was the founder of Edmonton's Heritage Festival which annually
attracts some 400,000 participants to Hawrelak Park in Edmonton South, a park which indeed was named after Edmonton's first mayor of Ukrainian origin.
The second individual who will become a Member of the Order of Canada is Mrs. Mary Lobay, descendant of one of the first pioneer Ukrainian families to settle in rural agricultural Alberta. Mrs. Lobay is indeed the surviving sister of the distinguished late Mayor of Edmonton, William Hawrelak, after whom the aforementioned park was named.
The third individual, Dr. Henry Kreisel, will be made an Officer of the Order of Canada on May 6. Dr. Kreisel is a distinguished Canadian author, novelist and most recently has delivered to the Minister responsible for multiculturalism a very interesting, creative and imaginative plan for the cultivation of heritage languages in our country. What is remarkable is that no one is even taking notice of their multiculturalism symbol because, at least in my city, multiculturalism is a fact of life in which we glory.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) has made the point that sometimes we do not recognize when we are walking through history. That is exactly what is happening right now. Giving legislative expression to Canada's multicultural and multiracial reality is a landmark event. It is an event for the history books, rooted in the everyday life of the Canadian people.

Bill C-93 represents a landmark in the evolution of our society. This legislation, while reminding us that multiculturalism is as old as Canadian society itself, at the same time emphasizes that it is also one of our most innovative enterprises. Furthermore, it bears witness to the determination and strength of those men and women who helped to build this great country we have become.

Our aboriginal peoples were the first citizens of this nation. They survived in a harsh and unpredictable natural environment by creating a strong spiritual life, and a mythology which is part of our collective sense of being Canadian. No doubt, many Hon. Members are aware that an outstanding exhibition of native arts and artifacts called "The Spirit Sings: Artistic Traditions of Canada's First Peoples" was assembled at the Glenbow Museum at Calgary as a showpiece of the Calgary Winter Olympics. It unveiled for the world the richness and diversity of aboriginal culture in Canada.
When the French and the British first arrived in this country they made contact with an aboriginal society which was both multicultural and multilingual. That essential reality of Canadian identity was intensified by pioneers of many different origins who came to forge a new future for themselves in this land of promise and opportunity.

As the Prairies were settled and our transportation centres grew into cities, we sought our farmers and labourers wherever we could find them. The list of their homelands, languages and cultural traditions is almost limitless. Their courage, endurance and dreams for a better life left a permanent legacy in every community across Canada; not the least of those legacies was tolerance.
A historic attachment to the land is part of the cultural heritage of all Canadians. It is shared by our aboriginal peoples, by courageous European pioneers, Sifton's men in sheepskin coats, Ukrainians, Poles, Germans and many others who dug deep into Canadian soil to create fertile fields, strong communities and their own special experience of being Canadian.
That experience is shared by those who helped open up this land from sea to sea. As we are all aware, the incredible task of building the Canadian Pacific Railway through the Canadian Shield, over the Prairies, down the treacherous Fraser Canyon could never have been done without the backbreaking effort of labourers from all corners of the globe, especially Chinese Canadians.

Canada did not become a multicultural nation overnight. Multiculturalism is a factor that has always been present in the course of our history. It is a factor that has greatly influenced our concept of human rights and equality among citizens. In Canada, we cannot tolerate any form of racism. Both socially and legally, discrimination and intolerance are attitudes that to us are unacceptable. It is ideals such as these which over the years have attracted and still attract people from all over the world to this country.

In the late eighteenth century roughly 50,000 American residents moved to what is now Canada during the revolutionary war, becoming known as United Empire Loyalists. In the nineteenth century, prior to Abraham Lincoln's emancipation proclamation, thousands of black Americans travelled north on the famous underground railroad to seek their freedom in Canada. In this century Canada has continued to provide refuge and a fresh start to hundreds of thousands of people fleeing oppression.
Multiculturalism is a working reality in our society, a welcome fact of our daily life. However, there was a time when severe doubts were expressed about the possibility of turning what some called a "motley crowd of immigrants" into a nation of Canadians. A young Methodist minister named J.S. Woodsworth, later the founder of the CCF Party, ran his All People's Mission in Winnipeg in the early 1900s. Surveying the scene around him with a mixture of pride and apprehension, he wrote in 1909:
English and Russians, French and Germans, Austrians and Italians,
Japanese and Hindus-a mixed multitude, they are dumped into Canada by a
kind of endless chain. They sort themselves out after a fashion, and each seeks
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
to find a corner somewhere. But how shall we weld this heterogeneous mass into one people? That is our problem.
As we approach the twenty-first century, the people and the Government of Canada have found ways to address that problem with caring and with imagination. One of them is the Bill that we are debating today.
We have come to understand that being largely a nation of immigrants, or descendants of immigrants, gives us a unique perspective on the world, and it gives us an appreciation of the strength and vitality generated by our cultural and racial diversity.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said so well when he addressed the Canadian Multilingual Press Association last October:
The magnificence of our citizenship has been powerfully enriched by our multicultural reality. This reality is part of our life, of who we are, of what we can become.
Bill C-93 gives legal substance to this Government's conviction that multiculturalism lies at the heart of our Canadian identity. This conviction was definitely lacking in the Liberal Bill C-48, as was much else of any substance. What that Bill proposed was a loose amalgam, a celebration of differences. Our Bill enables a catalyst which will aid in the creation of the new Canadian alloy, a sum much stronger than the aggregation of its parts.
When passed, our Canadian Multiculturalism Act will affirm in law that every Canadian can determine the extent to which he or she wishes to identify with, enjoy, enhance and share their previous heritage of birth and ancestry. It will promote multiculturalism as a central feature of our Canadian society and it will reflect our conviction that, regardless of origin, every Canadian citizen has an equal chance to participate in and contribute to the social economic, cultural and political life of this nation.
We as a nation are committed to the idea that all Canadians, wherever they are born, whatever their roots, are entitled to an equal chance. They have a right to be educated, trained, to choose their life's work and to be able to benefit from its rewards. There must be no barriers to ensuring that these things hold true to all Canadians of every origin.
It has been asked why there is no ministry in this Bill and no commissioner of multiculturalism. I submit that if we were doing it again and were not operating in the milieu of paternalism, which perhaps necessarily prevailed in the nineteenth century, we would not recreate a Department of Indian Affairs. Let us not be patronizing with multiculturalism today. Let us inculcate everything we do with the spirit that whatever minister takes the oath office, whatever officer or head of a Crown agency or corporation takes office, whatever member of a board of directors takes an oath of office, he or she subscribes to the multicultural reality and multicultural glory of Canada. Only then can we ensure that we have more Cabinet ministers with names like those of the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), the Hon. Minister of National Health and

Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Welfare (Mr. Epp), and the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski), and more lieutenant governors like Lincoln Alexander and more premiers whose origins we celebrate, if not their policies, like Joe Ghiz and Bill Vander Zalm. We can ensure that all future athletes of all racial or cultural origins, such as sprinter Ben Johnson, diver Sylvie Bernier or equestrian Ian Miller will be able to realize their full potential.
I am sure Hon. Members will agree, however, that the vitality and richness of our multicultural diversity in action is not found only in our sports or political arenas. It is found in all the activities of our neighbourhoods, large centres and small communities all across Canada. The shops, restaurants, and small businesses run by members of our ethnocultural groups contribute in large part to this country's economic prosperity. According to census data for 1981, half of the small businesses in Canada are owned and operated by members of our cultural or racial minority groups. However, economics aside, it is evident that multicultural enterprises add the kind of variety, vitality, and interest to our downtown cores which help to animate our cities.

Formerly, multiculturalism was associated with folk dancing, national costumes or international cuisine. Celebrations and ceremonies held by a cultural community were basically the business of the people of that community. The situation has changed somewhat today, when we see a kind of symbiosis, where sharing and mutual appreciation are becoming increasingly important.

I recall a remarkable event which could have happened only in Canada at the celebration of India Day last year when a Ukrainian dance troupe performed a Punjabi harvest dance. That is more than symbiosis. Summer gatherings such as the Ukrainian Pysanka Festival in Vegreville, Edmonton's magnificent Heritage Days, Saskatoon's Folkfest and Winnipeg's Folklorama, or Toronto's Caribana and the countrywide Chinese New Year's celebrations are now part of the Canadian calendar of special events. Each year they attract more and more Canadians of all backgrounds and races as well as increasing numbers of visitors, visitors who recognize that this is what is uniquely Canadian.
I had the privilege in 1986 of being called upon on very short notice, in fact 30 seconds, to give a 15-minute talk on Canada and what it means to be Canadian. This talk was to be delivered half way around the world as I was visiting the province of Negros Occidental in the Philippines at the time. I had the advantage of having to wait for the simultaneous into the Ilongo language to finish, giving me an opportunity to gather my thoughts.
I chose to talk not about the stereotypes of Canada, the northern nation, the vast nation which is not quite the United States. I chose to talk about multiculturalism and celebrated the fact that while many countries in our world are multicultural through forces of invasion or history, Canada is the only country, certainly the first country on the globe, to have chosen by active political will to become a multicultural society and to glory in it.
Earlier in this debate the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) implied that the Canada Council turns away applications from some Canadians because of their origins. I cannot understand where the Hon. Member got this idea. He should know better. Let me cite some evidence to the contrary. The Council has funded Punjabi and Chinese literacy projects, documentary films made by Inuit artists, and the publication of short stories written by Greek immigrants. The Council has funded a biography of pioneer black Canadian community leaders and the performances of black musicians in Nova Scotia.
I do not intend to dwell on long lists. My point is to emphasize the work that the Canada Council has already done. More will be done. The multicultural policy of Canada will apply to the Canada Council as a federal institution and I am certain that the Council will join all other federal institutions in celebrating and promoting the cultural and racial diversity of Canada.
I would like to emphasize that Bill C-93 is perfectly clear, not only about maintaining our commitment to the official languages of Canada, but also about preserving our heritage languages. The Bill states that the Government of Canada will "facilitate the acquisition, retention and use of all languages that contribute to the multicultural heritage of Canada".
As part of that commitment the multiculturalism sector of the Department of the Secretary of State recently sponsored a national heritage language teaching training conference in Toronto. The Government is currently considering new initiatives in the area of heritage languages. We are considering how a heritage language institute in Edmonton can best be established, based on the recommendations of the distinguished Dr. Henry Kreisel, and what its mandates and priorities should be.
We are examining the possibility of creating a national network which would link an Edmonton institute with the Language Resource Unit at the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education in Toronto and eventually to a complementary operation in Quebec.
Finally, we are asking the Assembly of First Nations to submit recommendations to the Government on the possible creation of an aboriginal languages institute.
All of this activity underlines the Government's belief that heritage languages are a vital element of communications and understanding in our multicultural society. Language is important to this country, not only in terms of social harmony

but also in an economic way for trade, for diplomacy, and for tourism.
A few years ago a government study analysed our tourism industry, particularly the question of why Americans come to Canada. We all assumed it was the snow-capped mountains, the rushing rivers, or the CN Tower, but that was not really the case. They said that they came because they appreciate the linguistic and cultural diversity of Canada. That was the number one reason given.

Mr. Speaker, this is being confirmed daily. Canada's distinctive character as a multicultural nation has made it a country that is enjoying healthy and dynamic growth both socially, culturally and economically. By putting to good use the knowledge, experience and talents of all these people who have come to this country from the four corners of the earth, we can greatly enhance Canada's potential in the areas of international trade and diplomacy and in the field of cultural and scientific exchange.

The Government believes wholeheartedly that a strengthened commitment to multiculturalism through Bill C-93 will add to our international stature. Multiculturalism is not only one of our most valuable natural resources, it is our gateway to the world.
I would like to extend personal congratulations to my hon. colleague, the Secretary of State, for bringing forth this historic legislation. I urge all Members of the House to respond quickly to the vision of the proposed Canadian Multiculturalism Act by giving it their full and unqualified support. This Bill is proactive. In fact, it has become a veritable Christmas tree, or Hanukkah bush, which offers choice and opportunity, not command and control.
In fact, only two weeks ago I was lobbied by the Canadian Conference for the Deaf and the Western Institute for Research into Deafness who put forth, with some vigour and some persuasiveness, the argument that the deaf ought to be embraced within the Multiculturalism Act. It is that attractive an Act. It is a joyful Act, Mr. Speaker.

I commend the Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Edwards) for bringing a degree of sincerity and passion to the debate. Nonetheless, I think that this individual, who is part of the Conservative Party, is prepared to put multiculturalism into deep freeze, is prepared, by embracing this Bill, to say that the future of multiculturalism is in the past.
The Member was very articulate in a number of his analogies. If he wants to use Christmas as an analogy, I suggest that this Bill is a beautifully gift-wrapped box, but when opened up there is very little inside. If you want to use the Olympic analogy, this legislation is pleased with a bronze rather than striving for gold.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
The Member began by addressing a number of different points. He said first that to talk of a separate ministry was to ghettoize multiculturalism. Why is he so quick to label a ministry as ghettoization? Why is it patronizing to develop bigger and more effective program delivery by bringing various programs, which are now spread throughout the federal civil service, under one roof? Why is it ghettoizing to have a larger budget under one roof than now exists in various departments? Why would it be ghettoization to have a full time Minister and a Deputy Minister which would obviously give additional political power and why if we cannot see this as one step towards one day having one ministry of culture, not communications and culture, but one department of culture whose message is that our culture is multiculturalism?
We cannot necessarily attain that goal with just a leap of faith that lands nowhere. If one subscribes to that more progressive longer-term vision, one can see this as one stepping-stone towards that eventual day. Why is that too seen as ghettoization?
Finally, Bill C-48 was not the answer. I am prepared to say that today. One of the first things the former Minister responsible for multiculturalism under the Tory administration did was to send a copy of Bill C-48 to all the groups across the country in order to get a consultative process under way. He asked how he could improve the Bill, how to take it one step further? In the interim, there was a standing committee that had as its basic premise, I suggest, a very strong and comprehensive multiculturalism Act. Unfortunately, today we have a multiculturalism bill that is no better than bill c-48, despite the intervening four years of consultations and a unanimous report from a committee. I want to know why the Tories' definition of a future is clearly in the past? If Bill C-48 was not good enough, why did we not make it better?

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted that the Liberal critic has entered into this debate, because it gives me an opportunity to tell him that history and events have not only undertaken the Government, but have more than overtaken the Liberal Party. The fact is that Canadians, however they describe themselves beyond their Canadianism, today recognize that Canada is a multicultural nation and that that reality does not need to have the ghettoization of a particular ministry.
Rather than just leave it at that, I think it is appropriate to indicate what can happen. The Hon. Member has been around government for some time. I know he advised a previous Minister and I think he may have had some considerable part in the drafting of Bill C-48. However, the fact is that events have evolved very rapidly. Today the very idea of shunting off responsibility for multiculturalism to a particular Minister is not enough.
The Hon. Member says he could be the advocate. The fact is that each and every one of us, through every hour of every day,

should be the advocate and the celebrator of multiculturalism. We do not need some kind of a side ministry with, let us be honest, a history of turnover of Ministers for multiculturalism, being a training ground for junior Ministers who either disappear or go on to greater things. The Hon. Member talked about the consultative process, and why did we not embrace the recommendations of the standing committee. The chairman of the standing committee intervened in the debate. Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the words of the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards) as he celebrated the cultural diversity of the City of Edmonton. It reminded me, of course, of the cultural diversity of the City of Thunder Bay, and I suppose so many of us know of our cultural diversity and want to say good things about it. However, we need more than just words.
I want to focus more particularly on what the Hon. Member said in speaking of the way in which Bill C-93 gives legal substance to the Government's convictions regarding multiculturalism. The Member speaks of the way in which it might provide a catalyst to achieve a Canadian alloy. That is an image I am not so sure about. Too many people have been merged and assimilated in the alloying process. What we want in a policy on multiculturalism is to step back somewhat and allow the kind of freedom the Member noted the Bill provides for, giving people the opportunity to maintain cultures while being good Canadians.
The Member says the Liberals are looking to the past, implying there is a future to be grasped. He talks about the need for legislation to do that, but how can he find any
satisfaction in Bill C-93, which does nothing to develop the machinery? The Bill is inadequate. The worst judgment to render on this Bill is to say it institutionalizes the status quo. Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join my voice to those who have addressed the issue of multiculturalism in our society. We have heard some very warm, concerned and considered remarks from our colleagues from all sides of the House. That speaks well for the vision of tomorrow which is building through the ongoing steps involved in multiculturalism.
I see in the House my colleague, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer) with whom I had the pleasure of studying Section 15 of the Canadian Constitution, and the Charter of Rights. At that time we were looking at equality for all, which was just another step, another building block in our concern for non-discrimination and integration for all people on a fair and equitable basis as part of the Canadian ethos.
In retrospect, what we have been doing over the past number of years has been building. I had hoped that when we finally took the important step to enact our nation's historic commitment to multiculturalism that we would be looking at a Bill, such as Bill C-93 which is before us, and judge that Bill on the basis of its quality, its substance and the extent to which it enhances multiculturalism across Canada. That is a goal which all Members of the House hold dear. It is what they represent when they stand to speak as the elected representatives of their ridings. I know of very few ridings in the country that are not a reflection of the true multicultural and bilingual qualities that make up the Canada of today.
Creating a legislated framework for Canada's multicultural policy is therefore in itself a positive and valuable initiative. We have travelled a long road to arrive at this point. My colleague pointed out the role played by the late Prime Minister Diefenbaker. He also pointed out the role played by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). Add those names to the names of Liberal Prime Ministers and one sees that this has been an ongoing and growing concern for many, many years.
We cannot argue with the developments that we have made as a society that understands and respects our many diverse peoples. But moving forward and building on past initiatives in this vital area of national policy is the duty not only of the Government but of Members on all sides of the House.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that despite the problems that exist with Bill C-93 and the newspaper coverage and the remarks of editorialists which indicate serious concern about the content of the Bill, that is not the view with respect to the thrust of the Bill. I do not think we can miss the chance to protect our multicultural tradition through legislative action, for this is an ideal that has been pursued by many modern societies. I think that Canada with this as a legislated direction may be the first to put it into legalistic form.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
It represents a commitment to the recognition of the many ethnic groups that make up our nation's diverse population. For example, Canada is a nation with a rich history of accepting peoples from many and varied ethnic origins and, hopefully, having them become part and parcel of what we call or perceive as mainstream Canada.
We are supposed to be establishing a framework in law for Canada's strong and long-standing multicultural policy, a policy that states that we accept differences based on race, religion, language, modes of livelihood and regions of origin or habitat. Since we are all differentiated from one another on the basis of some of those factors, we all may be described as ethnics. Therefore cultural diversity, like individual differences, must be accommodated within the framework of political freedom.
Our democratic ideal supports this idea of accommodation. Our pluralistic society requires it. The 1982 Canadian Constitution mandates recognition of our multicultural heritage.
One root of Canada's multiculturalism policy was the 1963 Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism which was originally aimed at reviewing the status of the two founding peoples of Canada. An additional facet was added to the commission's task to examine the contribution made by other ethnic groups for which the cultural enrichment of Canada can be thanked, and the measures which could be taken to safeguard that contribution. This additional directive which came as an afterthought has in retrospect proven to be valuable for getting the ball rolling on Canada's multiculturalism policy.
By 1971 the Liberal Government committed Canada to a multicultural policy, but within a bilingual framework. In his statement Prime Minister Trudeau noted that although there are two official languages there is no official culture, nor does any ethnic group take precedence over any other. This was really the first formal recognition of the fact that every Canadian is an ethnic of some variety and each of our cultures deserves respect.
With these statements, multiculturalism emerged from its status as a mere fact of Canadian life to become an issue for full and active discussion on the nation's public policy agenda. We must now look at how these very heterogeneous social groupings, which are a reality in our society, can be recognized as part of the basic strands that form the warp and woof of the tapestry that is found by the weaving of the fabric that is Canada.
The reality of multiculturalism's new place on the agenda of national debate and action was confirmed by the then Prime Minister's comments on the need for official support from Government that would contribute to a richer life for us all. We all start with small things and grow. Now is the time to consolidate a dispersed growth into one concrete area so that we can look at what is happening and move the whole issue forward.

Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Fortunately, along with the words of the Prime Minister, about official support at that time, action did follow. The Government's actions included the establishment of a multiculturalism directorate within Secretary of State in 1971 and the appointment of a Minister of State for Multiculturalism in 1972. That was solid action, the kind of action that is missing in Bill C-93.
In 1977 Parliament passed the Canadian Human Rights Act which established the Human Rights Commission that could receive and investigate complaints of discrimination and develop programs that would combat discriminatory practices. Again, that was solid action, something more than the dreamy promises that we have in this Bill.
In 1982 the Canadian Constitution included multiculturalism, as well as Section 15, the equality and non-discriminatory clause, within our constitutional framework. There was a commission report, "Equality Now", and then a Bill, the beginning of a legislative framework.
In 1985 the House of Commons Standing Committee on Multiculturalism was established to act as a forum for ethnic community representations and to review the Government's progress in implementing multiculturalism policy, again, continuing a tradition of active not passive public policy with regard to multiculturalism.
This is not the first time that we have seen legislation in the House to support multiculturalism. As I previously stated, on June 21, 1984 the Government of the day, through its Minister, David Collenette, introduced Bill C-48, the Multiculturalism Act. Unfortunately, it died on the Order Paper when a federal election was called in the fall of that year.
The last action by Members of Parliament prior to the introduction of Bill C-93 was the report of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Multiculturalism in June, 1987. This was the product of many hours of careful thought and consultation by our colleagues on that committee. I wish to pay particular respect to and congratulate my colleague, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), for his leadership and his open and active participation.
A creative and open-minded report flowed from the deliberations of this committee. It urged the enactment of a multiculturalism Bill, the creation of a new line department with a full-time senior cabinet Minister, the establishment of a commissioner, and the increase of budgets for related programs, much like that found under the Official Languages Bill. If we wish the bilingual character of Canada and its distinctiveness throughout this land to become a reality, then we have to put some action and some concrete policies into place. The same is true with respect to multiculturalism; it is the other side of the coin that makes up this wonderful Canada of ours.
The Government's official response accepted the basic tenets of the committee's report, but concluded that a new department and Minister were not needed. On the contrary, it seems to me that few ethnocultural groups would reject the appointment of a full-time Minister who could respond to their needs and assure them of due respect and attention at the Cabinet table. This Minister could not handle this whole task by himself. He needs the collaborative efforts at the Cabinet table of all the different Ministers who have roles and responsibilities to ensure multiculturalism together with the bilingual nature of Canada.
Nor would a commissioner be the wrong approach. It is vital that we have a commissioner who would report to Parliament on the progress we are making in this new and very vital area of our Canadian social reality. We need to find ways to harmonize our varying societies, develop mutual respect, and reduce social tensions through active progressive programs. We need to educate our society from childhood through adulthood. We need to remove discrimination due to ignorance and misunderstanding. We need to move into a pluralistic Canadian society on the basis of equality of opportunity for all, and have access to jobs based on skills and competence, irrespective of race or creed. That is one of the thrusts that is needed and is missing in terms of action guidelines.
That brings me to the legislation that we are now considering. If we are to achieve the true spirit envisaged in this Bill, we must find concrete ways for many ethnic communities to participate fully in Canadian society, rather than remaining on the fringes as is so often the complaint. Song and dance as part of the over-all practice is only one aspect of a full multicultural philosophy which is the reality of the Canada in which we live. Private and public institutions should reflect the true make-up of the population.
This is not reflected on the screens of this land, either on television screens, at the boards of directors, and certainly not in the films that we see in the theatre. Unfortunately Bill C-93 does not go far enough to actively strengthen and ensure the visibility of all ethnic groups in Canada.
This is not only the view of those of us in the Official Opposition. Mr. Lewis Chan of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council has called Bill C-93 "a shining symbol, and certainly a step forward, but it is a symbol without substance". How can it be otherwise for its goals are couched in general principles and objectives in cautious language terms. We see words like "should", "may", "facilitate", "encourage", but there is no enforcement mechanism, much like Bill C-62 which includes all the correct words around employment equity, but has no action, no mandatory or obligatory forward movement in the Bill.
There are more complaints. The Ontario Advisory Council on Multiculturalism and Citizenship has criticized the Government's decision not to establish a full-time ministry of
March 22, 1988

multiculturalism. They find it "unacceptable and it demonstrates the lack of leadership commitment for multiculturalism as a fundamental goal for Canada".
One of the biggest problems in this Bill is its lack of true enforceability. As I stated, my Party is only one of the many voices expressing this concern. We support the steps this legislation suggests "should" be taken by the Government to enhance Canada's multicultural life, but we believe it should state "shall" take those steps. It lacks specific implementation and enforcement provisions. That is the serious deficiency of this proposed Act.
I return to make the point I made at the beginning of my comments today. This Bill will be judged on the extent to which it actually enhances multiculturalism across the country. That is what Canadians are looking for-action and not promises. It does not take the bold step forward that we need. It does not require government action to implement the very policies it seeks to provide in this legislative framework. In the Bill the gap between policy and implementation is evident. I hope it is not a lack of good faith and goodwill. I hope we see the mechanisms to improve this Bill when it goes to committee.
There is no designated full-time cabinet Minister. There is a failure to do so, which will do little to open the doors of the federal Government to Canada's ethnocultural communities. This change would have gone a long way to improving dialogue between government and Canada's ethnic communities, giving them the attention that they deserve. Right now we are living in a time of great stress. It is very important that we reduce racial tensions, as we look at what is going on in society, and improve the general atmosphere. It is a very important concern.
As a nation, if we are going to take that large step forward that we require, which means encouraging all our ethnic groups to take pride in their Canadianism, which we would hope they would do while still retaining their attachment and pride in their own roots, this is absolutely key and fundamental. It is important that we encourage peoples of a variety of cultures to grow and retain their own identity while joining and enjoying celebrations with Canadians of different ethnic origins. Canada's collective identity would be enriched and reinforced.
While Canada is officially bilingual, that is, it has two languages, its cultural is multicultural. In Montreal this past Sunday I was struck at the time of the St. Patrick's parade that the crowd was very mixed. It reminded me of a festival parade last summer organized by the city's Caribbean black community in which I was actively involved. The crowd was also very varied. These celebrations by the very diverse ethnic cultural minority communities have become part of the pluralistic community celebrations of the Canadian mosaic. People of all ethnic minorities gathered around, joined in, showed tolerance, understanding, and appreciation of Canada.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
They thought of this as a normal relationship in the pluralistic society that is the reality of Canada today.
Because of the growing racial tensions that we are also feeling, there needs to be the legislative cadre in order that we can truly move forward. Bill C-93 is a fairly short piece of legislation. Clause 3 is a statement of the proposed multicultural policy, but it is largely a reiteration of the types of policies which were enunciated by successive federal Governments. It represents no dramatic breakthrough.
Another difficulty is that Clause 3 contains a number of intentions with regard to multicultural policy, but the good intentions are in no way followed through by commitments to actions. In effect we have a Bill which represents a statutory declaration of policy. It does not legislate any call to action by the Government.
As was indicated by the largest coalition of ethnic organizations, the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, the word "should" is one of the weakest aspects of the whole Bill. A commitment would be indicated by "shall" or even by "must". The word "should" leaves it totally optional with regard to whether various federal institutions will do what they are called upon to do.
The Bill respecting the Official Languages Act is an example of the way in which the multiculturalism Bill could have been drafted to ensure action by the federal Government. In so doing it would have given much more hope to Canada's many ethnocultural organizations. Instead, the Bill simply places into law mere suggestions of what Governments could do to build and strengthen the multicultural fabric which is our reality.
In conclusion, while we all applaud the initiative of the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) and favour the principles of multicultural equality which the Bill embodies in spirit, the fact is that many members of the Canadian ethnocultural community find, as do we in the Official Opposition, that the Bill does not meet the test. We want to ensure that our multicultural society is just a normal fact of life. We need the kinds of actions which will build a strong and meaningful multicultural Act and will provide the kind of tolerance to move our multicultural society and its communities into mainstream Canadian life.
I suggest that we do not just want promises to be legislated, we want the eventual goal of true equality for all. Let us not promote another Bill of missed opportunities. The employment equity Bill, which was to address discriminatory practices but had no teeth, was a lesson. Let us learn from that mistake and demand that Bill C-93 become a proactive Bill so that it will give substance to and enhance the basic fabric of our society- multiculturalism.

March 22, 1988
