speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rose in my seat earlier to comment on the speech by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). Unfortunately, I think you do not see me.
First of all, I would like to congratulate my colleague and also the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards) for a very interesting speech, and I may add I was most interested in what he had to say about multiculturalism and the aboriginal people especially, because I had the pleasure of spending part of last week in that beautiful part of Canada we call the Yukon.
Mr. Speaker, if you have no objection, I would also like to correct and in fact respond to a false impression given by my socialist colleague of the New Democratic Party from Vancouver East, and I quote: "That aboriginal people are considered as ethnic groups." Mr. Speaker, I feel obliged to correct this statement for the benefit of the House.

I agree that the culture and languages of the Canadian aboriginal peoples are rooted in this land. They are a living expression of an age old tradition. However, she seemed to feel that the new legislation could be interpreted as relegating Canada's aboriginal peoples to the status of just another ethnic group. Nothing could be further from what we intended.
The preamble to the Bill refers to the constitutional recognition of the rights of Canada's aboriginal peoples. It is our belief that the cultural and racial diversity of Canada is our greatest national strength. We did not want to make it appear-
Is this question for me?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I will get to it. I just wanted to make some points for clarification.
This is why the reference is therefore intended to send a message on the unique position of the aboriginal peoples of Canada in the context of diversity.
I visited the Yukon this past weekend. I want to ask my colleague whether she agrees with the Hon. Member on the following issue, and I will quote her again:

... "aboriginal people are considered as ethnic groups". So I want to ask the Hon. Member whether or not she thinks there is a difference between ethnic groups and aboriginal people. I want to ask the Hon. Member whether we were right to correct her.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the Hon. Member finally got to me. I was wondering whether he would address some of the issues which concern me. Nevertheless, I will address the issue that seems to be concerning him.
As I said at the outset of my remarks, the fabric and tissue of Canada is the warp and the woof which form Canada today-its multicultural constituencies.
I would say that there are no majority groups left in Canada, not the Wasps, the Anglophones, the Francophones, the Quebegois, the Indian peoples, the aboriginal peoples, or the Eskimos, as we used to call them, or the Inuit, and I would say this of the Ukrainians in the West and the Italians in the East. No matter what group the Hon. Member would care to identify, we are all minorities within the majoritarian society that is the Canada in which we are building toward a tolerant, wonderful, and understanding society.
It is not a matter of isolating the aboriginal peoples who were among the founding nations of the land, nor is it a matter of isolating the English and the French who came here to share this beautiful place; I would say that all those who came, whether it was the Hon. Member's Italian ancestors or my Jewish ancestors, are all the same. We are building toward a fine future together.

Mr. Speaker, let me just observe, partly in defence of the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), that the Parliamentary Secretary has made a vital mistake in being critical of labelling any group as "ethnic". The point he misses is that multiculturalism recognizes diversity in the country including the aboriginal peoples. Respect for their rights and their desire to maintain communities on reserves, in bands, and through self-government can easily be seen as part of the advance of a multicultural society in Canada. I wish that he and his colleagues in government would recognize that.
Referring to the fine speech made by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), I should like to deal with something that should involve us these days. Let me break the silence in the House on the shooting of a young black man in Montreal, something about which we should have spoken earlier. I want to do that now and ask her, in the moment before we rise, whether she would have any thoughts about how the Parliament of Canada and the Government of Canada could be involved in a particular matter which strikes so many people. Despite the findings of an inquiry, or perhaps a jury trial, it strikes one that there are still dimensions of race to the issue.
What could we in the Parliament of Canada do to try to transcend these feelings in our country, particularly about this tragic situation in the City of Montreal?

Mr. Speaker, this was a tragedy for the family. The loss of a child or any member of a family, irrespective of circumstances, always causes heartache. In this instance, where we had what was perceived to be racial discrimination, the situation was even more difficult. The police officer in question was found not guilty.
To be in a position where one is perceived as dominant and uncaring as a result of whether an act was pre-thought or not
March 22, 1988

is not the issue. We are living in a society with racial tension, not just in Montreal but right across the land. Visible minority groups are subject to discrimination in a much much more overt way. That is why I spoke to education in my remarks about the need for tolerance in our society. We have not had the degree, number or right mix.
Thirty different ethnic minority groups live in my riding, from five or six very distinct visible minority differences. Policemen on duty, the Armed Forces, everyone has to learn how to live in a far more sensitive way in this environment. We have not learned that sensitivity to the same degree. We have not changed our approaches in the kinds of ways that we must. Even to the way we recruit recruits we use the wrong kind of criteria. We need to see all these minorities reflected in our society at every level. If people do not see them reflected, and if people do not become role models and others have no one to identify with then they feel oppressed. That is what is happening in Montreal. There is a feeling of oppression because people do not see themselves reflected at all levels of society. It is sad and we must do something about it. This Bill does not move constructively enough in that direction.

subsubtopic: LACK OF SUPPORT FOR SOCIAL AND COMMUNITY NEEDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Allan Taylor, Chairman of the Board of the Royal Bank of Canada, has provided a most remarkable and convincing rationale for a significant increase in corporate income taxes. Mr. Taylor, in a forceful speech to the Montreal Chamber of Commerce, noted that when it comes to financial support to meet social and community needs, Canadian companies are falling down.
He said that Canadian companies give less as a percentage of pre-tax earnings than they did 20 years ago, and that 90 per cent of them give nothing at all. In 1969, corporate donations as a percentage of pretax profits were just under 0.8 per cent. In 1985, the figure had slipped to 0.5 per cent. INTERNATIONAL DAY FOR THE ELIMINATION OF RACIAL DISCRIMINATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I offered a few words in commemoration of the Sharpeville massacre of 28 years ago. I did not mention that the anniversary of that event had been declared by the United Nations as International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.
Although Canada, in observing that event, can be proud of the progress it has made in this respect, we still have much to accomplish. This was dramatized by the protest demonstration in Montreal last Saturday where 1,000 Canadians marched in memory of Anthony Griffin and demanded that the Province of Quebec act with dispatch to end discrimination and to ensure equality of treatment for all racial minority groups.
It is important that no province be allowed to override the Charter provisions ensuring racial equality, and it is important too to insist that no province, however distinct, fail to implement the guarantee that Canada provides only one kind of citizenship, and that must be first class.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ESTABLISH ADAPTATION PROGRAM FOR OLDER WORKERS
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ESTABLISH ADAPTATION PROGRAM FOR OLDER WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday morning I had the pleasure of meeting with several senior citizens clubs from the riding of Montreal- Sainte-Marie, and also with a group of workers between the ages of 40 and 65. These people are disappointed and find it unacceptable that the Conservative Government has abolished the Program for Older Worker Adjustment, under which workers in the textile, footwear and apparel industries between the ages of 55 and 64 were entitled to take early retirement.
Unfortunately, in November 1986 this Government abolished the program in favour of a new program, but so far, nothing has been settled.
Mr. Speaker, I would therefore urge all Conservative Members to do their duty and put pressure on the Minister of Labour to reinstate the Program for Older Worker Adjustment as soon as possible so that all older workers in Canada will get a fair deal.

subtopic: CONDEMNATION OF USE IN IRAQ-IRAN WAR
CONDEMNATION OF USE IN IRAQ-IRAN WAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been a dangerous escalation in the Iraq-Iran war. Strong
evidence has emerged that confirms the use of chemical weapons. Such an escalation will lead to heavier casualties as well as increased terror among the innocent civilian population.
Chemical weapons were internationally banned in 1925 after their initial use in the First World War, due to the horrible effects these agents had on their victims. In addition, today's chemical weapons are complex chemical derivatives.
The use of these chemical agents raises the possibility of a future biological catastrophe for the region and perhaps for other nations which are not involved in this conflict. We in this House must use all the means at our disposal to prevent any more chemical weapons from being used and to see to a speedy end to this tragic conflict.

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, just after the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, I want to take up questions I asked three weeks ago regarding the actions of the External Affairs Department.
The Minister (Mr. Clark) and the Department of External Affairs have been interfering with the freedom of association and expression of Canadians. They have done this recently with regard to communities of Asian and Middle Eastern origin which are intensely concerned about the human rights of their compatriots in other countries.
It would appear that the Department of External Affairs has little regard for the freedom of association and of expression in our country when it comes under pressure from foreign Governments. Its preoccupation with trade opportunities leaves the Department dangerously open to pressure from these Governments to ostracize organizations and silence critics.
Canadians expect the Department of External Affairs to defend our interests. The protection of our ethnocultural communities and the advance of human rights everywhere are among our most vital national interests.
I call on the Minister to recognize these realities and to reform the way the Department of External Affairs responds to pressure from foreign Governments.
March 22, 1988

Mr. Speaker, in recent months we heard the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party of Canada saying that if they were running this country, they would be able to guarantee Canadians a full employment policy. We must remember it was because of the socialist and nationalist policies and the disincentives promoted by the New Democratic Party of Canada and implemented by the Liberal Party that this country experienced record unemployment levels in the seventies and the beginning of the eighties.
The people of the Quebec City area, especially those in the riding of Quebec East, are more than capable of implementing the proposals of the Conservative Party for dealing with this legacy of instability from the previous Liberal Government.
Employment is a priority for the Conservative Party, but we must also stress the creation of more stable and more gainful employment.
A return to greater reliance on the public sector as urged by the New Democratic Party and the Liberal Party of Canada would mean accepting unemployment as a necessary evil and leading this country into an era of social indifference, something Canadian men and women do not want.

subtopic: PRE-RETIREMENT LEAVE-PAYMENT OF UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE PREMIUMS
PRE-RETIREMENT LEAVE-PAYMENT OF UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE PREMIUMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring up once again the issue of preretirement leave at Cape Breton Development Corporation. The Devco PRL plan was designed to lay off workers before their normal retirement age of 65 so that some type of continuing remuneration could be offered to displaced workers. This meant, in effect, that these workers were still engaged under a contract of service to Devco and could therefore continue to earn entitlement to Canada Pension Plan benefits.
Since the PRL plan of 1971, many miners have now gone for a compassionate disability pension and programs under the Labour Adjustment Program. Under these programs, individuals were not being requested to pay unemployment insurance premiums. I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) to change this unfair and discriminatory deduction. A change would result in substantial savings for the workers involved.
On March 15, I received a response from the Minister. In it he states that this ruling will remain in effect until such time as Devco chooses to amend its plan. He then warns against Devco amending this plan because an amendment might jeopardize their continued entitlement to Canada Pension Plan benefits. Thus, the situation will remain as it is. The Minister and the Government have once again decided to do nothing, to the detriment of all the workers eligible for this plan at the Cape Breton Development Corporation.

Mr. Speaker, my constituency of Sarnia-Lambton is located on the shores of beautiful Lake Huron and the St. Clair River. We boast miles and miles of sandy beaches and are known throughout the area as "Blue Water Land".
We have acres of parkland and conservation areas, and are joined with our American neighbours by the Blue Water Bridge and the railway tunnel. For these, and a multitude of other reasons, my constituents and I are working hard and tirelessly to develop the tourism potential of our community.
As Sarnia-Lambton is within a day's travel of more than half of the U.S. population, much of our efforts have been directed toward the attraction of this tourist market. Similarly, the Government of Canada has recognized this huge potential market and is directing much of its tourism advertising budget to the United States.
Consequently, it was with great dismay that I discovered from the President of VIA Rail that the company has a policy of limiting the number of seats available for sale to American wholesalers.
I wonder whether the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Valcourt) is aware that, while we are expending tremendous effort to attract American visitors to Canada, VIA does not have enough equipment to carry all who wish to travel by rail at the times they wish to travel.

Mr. Speaker, for years many Canadians have asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) to permit their sons and daughters to enter Canada as family class immigrants even

March 22, 1988
after age 21 because family ties are very important in our culture.
At last the Minister agreed, on August 11, 1987. Further, on October 31 the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) promised to admit unmarried sons and daughters of any age as family class and to give five extra points to married children and brothers and sisters applying as assisted relatives. Yet, to this day, the Minister has neither kept his promise nor told us when he will.
In the same way, the former Minister of Justice promised two years ago to eliminate the unfair difference between citizens and permanent residents so that both groups would have equal rights to sponsor parents of any age. Yet to date the Government has not kept this promise.
I call on the Government to stop playing on the family loyalties of immigrant Canadians and bring these two promises into law.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of the Desjardins Movement's annual meeting held this week in Montreal, I have the privilege, as a Member of Parliament whose riding includes the headquarters of that tremendous financial co-op, to congratulate the 4,200,000 Quebecers who are members of the Desjardins Movement, to recognize the excellent work of the 28,500 Desjardins employees and to thank the 18,330 voluntary directors.
All members of that team are helping bring about every day a higher return for the Desjardins Movement's assets which are totalling $34 billion. Let Desjardins keep up the good work!

Mr. Speaker, 1981 was designated the International Year of Disabled Persons to focus attention on the needs, hopes, and talents of disabled people. A committee of Parliament produced a report entitled "Obstacles" with over 100 recommendations. That year also saw physical and mental disability prohibited as grounds of
discrimination under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The 1984 report of the Commission on Equality and Employment and the 1985 report of the parliamentary Committee on Equality Rights were followed in March, 1987, by another parliamentary committee report called "Challenge-Putting Our House in Order".
Many recommendations of all these reports, going right back to the "Obstacles" report, have yet to be implemented and a great deal of work remains to be done in integrating disabled people into the community. The Government should make this issue a priority and encourage all groups in society to take similar action.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to take this opportunity to speak on the contribution of the various ethnic groups in the development of Canada while Bill C-93 is being debated.
I would like to inform the House that my riding of Timmins-Chapleau has 14 ethnic groups living in it and they all get along well. In fact I believe the various communities within the riding serve as an example for all of Canada when it comes to tolerance, co-operation, and contribution by all toward an improved quality of life. These 14 groups have created a social fabric which is a role model for the nation.
Just as Bill C-93 recognizes in an official way the multicultural society in which we live, the communities in my riding have recognized and honoured those groups which have made such significant contributions toward their development. We are happy that Bill C-93 recognizes, preserves, and enhances the cultural and racial diversity of our great nation.

Mr. Speaker, today is the fourth anniversary to the day of a speech by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney), who was then the Leader of the Opposition, to the Chamber of Commerce in Montreal. On March 22, 1984, the Prime Minister said: "We are going to double our collective national commitment to research and development within the life of our first government mandate".
Not only has the Prime Minister not doubled our commitment, but research and development spending has gone down
March 22, 1988

as a percentage of gross national product. The Prime Minister of Canada should explain why he has failed so miserably to make progress toward that important goal which affects our ability to compete in world markets.
Not only has R and D spending gone down, but the Government has abandoned the goal about which the Prime Minister so eloquently spoke in 1984. The Prime Minister should explain why the Government has refused to commit itself to a target and a timetable for increasing research and development spending which means so much for jobs, for the competitiveness of the Canadian economy, and for the health of our whole country.

subsubtopic: THE NORTH-CANADIAN INSTITUTE OF INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS STUDY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my questions are directed to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister will know that yesterday a working group of the Canadian Institute of International Affairs released an extremely important study on the future of Canada's North. The group comprises a very distinguished number of first-rate Canadians.
The Prime Minister will also know that we on this side of the House took exception to the deal his Government signed with the United States permitting passage of American vessels through Canadian Arctic waters. We felt it was a weakening of Canadian sovereignty and our claims to Canadian sovereignty over those waters.
How does the Prime Minister respond to a conclusion on page 44 of the study of this working group which says: "the working Group is unable to agree with the opinion of the Prime Minister ..." that 'What we have now significantly advances Canadian interests'". How does the Prime Minister respond to this group of eminent Canadians who contradict him on the effect on Canadian sovereignty of the recent agreement signed with the United States?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, Canadians are free to disagree with the position of the Government. I do not have to tell the Leader of the Opposition about freedom to disagree. He is acquainted with it every day in his own Party and in his own caucus.

Member refers, which was indeed made by eminent Canadians, some of them with a long interest in the Canadian North. The Right Hon. subtopic: THE GREAT NORTH-CREATION OF INTERNATIONAL COUNCIL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister, through his own Secretary of State for External Affairs, did not respond to my suggestion

March 22, 1988
Oral Questions
that a new international regime be created for the Arctic, and the Minister of National Defence did not react constructively to the proposition made by Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbatchev.
What is the response of the Prime Minister-or the Secretary of State for External Affairs, if you will-to the recommendation made by this Canadian private sector group of experts that Canada should take the initiative of convening all countries interested in the Arctic with a view to creating an international council to settle questions related to the nordic regions? speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: THE GREAT NORTH-CREATION OF INTERNATIONAL COUNCIL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this is an interesting, serious and important recommendation concerning co-operation in the North, co-operation with other Arctic countries. Indeed our Government took a number of initiatives and, for the first time we took the position that we ought to establish Canadian sovereignty in the North. We as a Government are prepared, for the first time-I cannot make the same comment about the administration of the Right Hon. the Leader of the Opposition-to recognize the jurisdiction of a world tribunal with respect to our sovereignty in the North. He is talking about cooperation with other countries involved in the Arctic. As he would know, last November I attended a meeting in Tromso, in Norway, to discuss and take the very kind of initiatives that have just been suggested.
Mr. Speaker, for a long time the North was ignored by Liberal Governments. This Government has established a strong sovereign Canadian interest in our North.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have to do anything more than recite the gentlemen who contributed to this particular report in rebutting the statement just made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
On this side of the House we have always stressed the need for a co-ordinated federal approach, that is to say, a closer coordination of federal Departments in dealing with the North and with the people of our North.
The Prime Minister, despite our pleas, has always argued that there has been sufficient co-ordination to that purpose under his Government. Would the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs be willing to comment on a statement found in the Canadian Institute of International Affairs Working Group's report found on page 66 which states:
-developments in recent years have been and continue to be in the reverse direction, with a weakening and loss of mechanisms to ensure a comprehensive
information base for northern policy and for its implementation. The Working Group strongly urges that immediate attention be given to establish effective interdepartmental co-ordination without which a coherent total policy for the Arctic will not be possible.
Those words are clear enough for the Secretary of State for External Affairs to respond in explaining why it is that his Government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister, has failed to develop a co-ordinated approach to our northern problems and to our Arctic.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Government under the leadership of the Prime Minister has shown a more active and constructive interest not only in the problems of northern Canadians but also in Canada's sovereign claims than was the case with former Governments.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. It concerns the interest rate policy of the Government.

March 22, 1988

Mr. Speaker, I would be the last person to try to interpret headlines for opposition Members. I think that in Mr. Crow's press conference after the release of the Bank of Canada report yesterday he made it quite clear what the policy of the Bank of Canada is, a policy which is supported by the Government of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is quite simple. Since the Minister is claiming that the signal is quite clear, my question is this: Which of the two newspaper articles reflects the policy of the Government? Should we expect the Canadian Government monetary policy to endorse lower interest rates and a Canadian dollar value more consistent with the needs of our exporters, or should we expect a high interest rate policy?
Mr. Speaker, you will remember that on March the 3rd the Minister of Finance himself announced to our exporters that as soon as inflation would reach 4 per cent, interest rates would come down. My question to the Minister is this: Which of the two newspaper headlines is right, and now that inflation has reached 4 per cent, are interest rates going to come down and reflect a slightly devalued Canadian dollar?

Mr. Speaker, I have made it clear, and the Governor of the Bank of Canada has made it quite clear that there are some signs of inflationary pressures in the economy today. He and I have both said that we believe it is important that we address those pressures before they become too strong and lead us into the problems that we experienced in the 1970s and early 1980s.
I have made the comment that it is a case of some preventive medicine now to avoid those problems. We have a strong economy. We have an economy that, in the last quarter of 1987, experienced the strongest growth of the year. We have seen investment intentions up over 17 per cent for 1988. We have seen job creation continue strong into 1988.
In the context of the strength in the economy and those inflationary pressures, it is important for us to address those pressures in the context of monetary policy.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Finance. I would like to pick up where he left off. Member had read the annual report of the Governor of the Bank of Canada he would have seen it very clearly stated in that report that the preoccupation of the Governor of the Bank of Canada is with the over-all health of the Canadian economy. The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Crombie that Bill C-93, an Act for the preservation and enhancement of multiculturalism in Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, in the course of this debate we have heard Members of the Opposition relate certain facts about the history of multiculturalism. However, since their interpretation was a very personal one, it may be misleading for some of our colleagues. That is why I think it is important, Mr. Speaker, to summarize the main points of this history on a strictly factual basis, remaining as objective as I possibly can.
As we all know, the policy on multiculturalism was adopted in 1971 by a unanimous resolution of Parliament. The following year, the Government created the position of Minister of State (Multiculturalism), and in 1973, the Department of the Secretary of State implemented its first multicultural grants program.
During the next ten years, the policy on multiculturalism remained practically unchanged, although the concept has changed considerably, especially in recent years. At the time, the policy was seen as a set of programs that were specifically and exclusively concerned with what was called, with some condescension, the "ethnic minorities", and their purpose was to help these minorities integrate harmoniously with Canadian society, while preserving their heritage.
Fortunately, this perception has gradually faded, and I think there are two reasons for this. We have had two major constitutional accords since then, and furthermore as we shall see, the Government in recent years has clearly shown its firm political will in this regard.
In 1982, the Parliament of Canada adopted the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms which provides: "This Charter shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians." Thus, multiculturalism was incorporated in the Constitution of Canada.
Last June, the First Ministers signed the now famous Meech Lake Constitutional Accord. Essentially, the Accord, which as you know, was approved by the Leader of the Official Opposition, recognizes that Quebec constitutes a distinct society within Canada, considering the French-speaking majority in this province.
The First Ministers insisted on reaffirming, in the same Accord the concept of multiculturalism set down in the Charter.
As the Prime Minister indicated last fall when speaking to the Canadian Ethnic Press Federation: "Nothing in the distinct society clause reduces or diminishes in any way the already recognized and established multicultural nature of the Canadian nation."
If our perception of multiculturalism has come a long way, it is also in large part due to this Government's efforts and, more precisely, to the Multiculturalism Program of the Secretary of State. As a matter of fact, when the Hon. Member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek), the present Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport, was appointed Minister of State for Multiculturalism in 1984, he set himself the goal of putting multiculturalism in the maimstream of Canadian society.
The Minister decided to give a new direction and a new perspective to our multiculturalism policy when he recognized a very simple fact, which is that all Canadians are immigrants or descend from immigrants. We are all proud to be Canadians but we are also proud of our roots and of the language, culture and traditions of our ancestors. From that perspective, we can all see that multiculturalism is everybody's concern and not only that of so-called "ethnic minorities".
In July 1986, when the Prime Minister appointed our colleague, the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) to his present position, he decided at the same time to merge the Secretary of State's responsabilities, which include Canadian citizenship, with those of the Minister responsible for Multiculturalism, in order to replace multiculturalism in the mainstream, at the heart of Canadian citizenship.
This extension of his mandate led the Minister to rethink our multiculturalism policy and to bring forward this Bill. Thus, for the Minister-and this is one of the basic ideas
March 22, 1988

behind Bill C-93-multiculturalism is a distinctive feature of our identity as Canadians and as a unique nation.
There are in fact, from the Minister's point of view, if I may be allowed to summarize his thoughts, three great pillars which shore up our originality and our identity as a nation. They are the following: multiculturalism, for the reasons which I have just outlined; also, our two official languages, French and English, which are among the most prestigious in the world today and which distinguish us clearly from other nations, and particularily from our neighbours to the South; and finally, Canadian citizenship, so admired and envied abroad, and which opens wide the doors of hospitality to Canadians who travel in other parts of the world.
For the government, this vision of Canadian identity is much more than theory. It is far more than rhetoric. In fact, each of these three components of our national identity is presently the object of legislation before Parliament.
On June 25 last, as you know, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) announced a renewed committment to official languages policy by presenting a Bill to amend and reinforce the Official Languages Act. Up to now, this Act had not been amended since it was adopted in 1969.
Also, the Secretary of State will soon present a bill to update the Canadian Citizenship Act. You will recall that last year the Minister issued a dicussion paper on the various aspects of the subject and invited Canadian citizens to share their opinions and comments with him.
Finally, of course, we have the Bill on multiculturalism which was introduced last December 1st by the minister responsible and which we are discussing today.
In essence, what the Government is trying to do is create a legal framework which would serve as a foundation for a much too fluid Canadian identity, which would solidify the constitutional guarantees related to official languages and which would also enhance our cultural heritage and equality of rights among all citizens.
I urge all Members as well as my colleagues to consider this Bill outside of political partisanship, I call upon their sense of pride as Canadians, to allow our country to take another step forward and turn a new page in our Canadian history.

March 22, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
examine hiring methods and to carry on recruitment campaigns specially targeted for visible minorities. The RCMP has also established an intercultural training program and has involved some of its senior members in efforts aimed at gaining a better understanding of ethnocultural as well as aboriginal communities.
It remains to be seen what effects those measures will have. Certainly, other initiatives have already produced very convincing results. As Hon. Members know or should know, small business is the cornerstone of Canadian economy and the major creator of new jobs since 1984. Our multicultural communities are driven by a strong entrepreneurial spirit and we can certainly say that entrepreneurs in these communities are among the most progressive, indeed the most dynamic in Canada.
In order to recognize that fact our government organized, in April 1986, a conference called Multiculturalism Means Business which was successful. It was the product of the joint efforts of the Secretariate of State, the Federal Business Development Bank, private sector business groups and community organizations.
Following that conference, the Ontario Office of the Federal Business Development Bank even established an ethnocultural advisory committee responsable for maintaining liaison between the various branches of the Federal Business Development Bank and the ethnic community small entrepreneurs.
Because of the direct action program of the Federal Business Development Bank, we can see today a large increase in the loans made by the Bank to members of cultural and racial communities other than those of our two founding nations. Other major centres have followed the example set by Toronto and I am convinced that their initiatives will have the same success.
Mr. Speaker, this first conference, which emphasized the contribution of multiculturalism, and the new Canadian Multiculturalism Act, which we have introduced, have something in common. Both recognize multiculturalism as one of the underpinnings of our Canadian society and believe in its major contribution to the prosperity of Canada. You yourself, Mr. Speaker, are a product of this multiculturalism, which is not only tolerated, but also encouraged in Canada as it brings to all of us a new cultural dimension, and is even financially profitable.
As the Hon. Members are certainly aware, federal efforts to revitalize and strengthen multiculturalism in Canada have been extremely successful. Indeed, our Government has already begun to apply the principles contained in this Bill and to keep the promises made in 1984. The adoption of Bill C-93 can only strengthen the commitment made by all our Departments.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention a few of the profitable initiatives undertaken jointly by various Departments in
compliance with the open-door multiculturalism policy of the federal Government.
Hon. Members will recall that, early in 1986, the Ministers responsible for Tourism, Communications and Multiculturalism decided to co-operate more closely by looking for means to harmonize their respective activities in their effort to reach a common goal. Next April, these three Departments will sponsor a conference on tourism, culture and multiculturalism, a first in Canada. This conference will examine the active role which our multicultural heritage can play in promoting Canadian tourism.
In addition, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), the Secretary of State and the Minister of State for Senior Citizens (Mr. Hees) are now organizing a major national conference on ethnic groups and their impact on our aging Canadian population.
Mr. Speaker, other federal departments have recognized the need for cultural diversity in our Canadian nation. For example, Parks Canada published information material and to make guided tours and diaporamas available in foreign languages; for example, in the Lachine Park, near Lasalle, Italian shows are available throughout the Summer.
Mr. Speaker, Parks Canada even conceived a very efficient marketing strategy by producing pamphlets in several language which were distributed during the 1988 Olympic Games in Calgary, where whe could welcome about all the cultures represented in the world.
In the same vein, Mr. Speaker, several initiatives focussing on the exchange of information are already bearing fruit. Just as an example, Elections Canada's booklet, Voting in Canada/Le vote au Canada, published in 16 languages, is now distributed across the country during citizenship swear-in ceremonies , which we had the opportunity to attend recently in Montreal and one of which was in LaSalle, for the 75th anniversary celebrations of our town.
I would also like to draw the attention of this House to the Fall 1987 issue of Reportage Canada, a quarterly published by the External Communications division of the External Affairs Department. As a matter of fact, this special issue on multiculturalism in Canada was distributed to some 60,000 opinion leaders across the world namely in the private sector, in the media, in educational establishments and to various Governments.
Mr. Speaker, these are only a few of our current initiatives.
I could single out others concerning multiculturalism, education, the preservation of ancestral languages, the growing awareness of medical and social services to the multicultural reality, and the establishment of guidelines on the image of minorities conveyed in federal communications.
Image, information and commitment are undoubtedly the key words of the new concept of multiculturalism and its contribution to the social, economic and cultural life of all Canadians.
March 22, 1988

Mr. Speaker, as I said even before Bill C-93 on multicultur-alism was first introduced, we had made considerable progress in our attempts to tailor Government programs to the requirements of the private sector, and these efforts also involved the federal public service.
In June 1986 our Government launched an affirmative action program designed to increase the representation of visible minority group members in the public service. More recently the Ministers involved with Treasury Board approved the establishment of quantitative goals in this respect so as to implement a real program, more than draft or theoretical projects shrouded by proposed legislation or pious wishes.
Still I should like to point out to Hon. Members that our Government did not saddle itself with a quota system, as some people had recommended. The quantitative goals set by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Mazankowski) are based on accurate Public Service Commission calculations. The Government is intent on reaching these goals through a recruiting and selection process whose only standard is the merit principle. Mr. Speaker, the idea is not to offer handouts to ethno-cultural communities, but to recognize their true value, both quantity-wise and quality-wise.
I believe that we all agree the best ways, respecting our Canadian ideal, to develop the wealth of our cultural and racial diversity are persuasion and representation rather than constraint and coercion, as was the case under the previous governments. This Bill on Multiculturalism is based on partnership and co-operation between the federal and provincial administrations on the one hand, and between the Government and the private sector on the other. It emphasizes participation, a participation of all individuals and cultural groups in our great country.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Multiculturalism Act now before you is directed at the whole Canadian society, without consideration of racial or cultural origin. It involves, therefore, all federal Departments, Ministers, business entities, community organizations and all Canadians. It enshrines the basic objectives of the Government's multicultural policy and ensures a solid legislative base for the programs aimed at implementing it.
Mr. Speaker, this legislation on multiculturalism describes the duties of the line minister and makes sure that Federal Departments as a whole meet their commitments and report to Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, it is for me a real privilege to be able to make these few remarks, as a representative of a riding where the majority is the sum of all minorities. In my riding there are Italians and Greeks. There is also a significant Portuguese community. We have Irish people who did put on a great show last week. There are French Canadians. There are people of British origin. There are Chinese. Recently, I had an opportunity to attend an ethno-cultural show presented by all the Francophone groups from Asia. I was quite surprised to hear
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
the great many people from Vietnam, especially among the older generation, talking about Indochina.
Mr. Speaker, multiculturalism is here. We must live it and stop thinking that it is an act of Government generosity. Our Government is involved. We accept the principle of Canadian multiculturalism by enshrining it in a legislation.
I note the Hon. Member has left.
Mr. Speaker, I made my exit too hastily. I did not expect any question. Could the Hon. Member repeat her question? I rushed back.

I have a question for the Hon. Member who spoke at some length in praise of this Bill. We certainly agree with the whole principle of multiculturalism. As the Hon. member probably knows, the criticism made by many groups, and which we would make, is that it is one thing to talk about principles and another thing to have ways of implementing those principles in solid programs with some real substance to assist multicultural groups in their efforts and also to effect government programs that are needed.
I wondered what the personal views are of the Hon. Member on the recommendation of the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism to have a department of multiculturalism with a full-time Minister, Deputy Minister, and a commissioner of multiculturalism to advocate programs that are needed and put some teeth into this in order that we could have much more substance to multiculturalism in Canada. What are the views of the Hon. Member on the question of having a department of multiculturalism with a commissioner, with research, and with all the things needed to really do a job in this field?

Mr. Speaker, 1 dealt with that in the main part of my speech. What we want is to go beyond lip service, statements of intent, by drafting legislation on which all Canadians will be able to rely to establish regulations or have solidly based recourse.
Secondly, we do not want any police. Why should we now consider the faults of multiculturalism? We should rather be promoting it.
Mr. Speaker, I think that is an old way of thinking. It was the same in the business world. Capital investment was limited instead of being encouraged. We plan to invite co-operation between people, not to police that co-operation through enforcement to coerce people to accept multiculturalism. Instead, we will help Canadians think it can be profitable, that there are business as well as cultural enrichments in multiculturalism.

March 22, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
So I think the legislation as proposed only sanctions what exists now, and I believe the Minister for Multiculturalism, who is accountable to this House, already has a monitoring role and will be quite free, about his department, to report to Parliament which remains the final enforcement authority in Canada.

Before we return to the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), I would like to give the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) an opportunity to ask his question. We will then return to the Hon. Member for Vancouver East.

The Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier) talks about the key word "enforcement" and translates that into what he would classify as policing. I wish to clarify that word, because it seems to be working itself into the Conservative vocabulary with increasing frequency.
The Member comes from a province that is obviously very sensitive to our official bilingualism policy. This Parliament is now engaged in updating official language legislation. Back in the 1960s when it was started by the then Prime Minister Trudeau, the centre-piece of official bilingualism did not only talk about bilingualism, did not only give us a beautiful, colourful, meaningful language that talked about this abstract notion, but he and his Government did something very profound about it. One of the things they did was to provide Parliament and the country with the very tools and mechanisms that would not only talk about bilingualism but that would deliver bilingualism.
Therefore, we did receive the bureaucratic structure that was able to meet the linguistic needs of our country. We did receive the appropriate Minister and Cabinet to talk with force. We established the proper enforcement mechanism, which consisted of the Commissioner for Official Languages, who made sure, without political constraint, that the commissioner would go through the federal bureaucracy and ensure that bilingualism was lived up to. If it was not, it was the duty of the commissioner to report to Parliament, not to the Government of the day, or to the Minister of the day who comes and goes, but to Parliament in order that all Canadians may see both the success stories and the warts within the system, and particularly, with regard to the latter, to encourage Governments and Parliaments to do something about it. If the Member supports the mechanisms that guaranteed official bilingualism in this country, such as a Commissioner for Official Languages, why is he so vividly opposed to trying to put in place similar mechanisms such as a commissioner in order that multiculturalism will not only be talked about but in fact lived up to and respected by Governments and institutions across the country?

Mr. Speaker, these are two completely different problems. The problem of multiculturalism is not the same thing as the legislation on bilingualism. The latter was so drafted as to include a Commissioner of Official Languages, the system has been tried and tested, and it fully meets the expectations of Canadians. Multiculturalism is an altogether different proposition. We had some difficulty trying to make people understand that the basic Canadian biculturalism and multiculturalism, or the enrichment we derive from ethnocultural circles, represent two systems or two entirely different notions. This is why we have two solutions to these two problems. Biculturalism as a solution does not apply to multiculturalism. First of all, they are two separate problems.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, again I stress that the basis of this Bill-and of all Bills introduced in the House, for that matter-is that people are expected to co-operate, they are invited, they are encouraged, and that is a far cry from the hard-line coercion and confrontation approach of the previous Government. And we all saw the ensuing mess. Mr. Speaker, our Government would rather urge Canadians to respect the law, we do not want the kind of negative legislation which tell them: Listen now, we are appointing a police force with which you will have to deal if you fail to do as we say. On the contrary, we will have people to urge Canadians to get involved and share in the wealth of multiculturalism. We in this Government are now determined to stress the positive rather than the negative aspects of legislation.
I regret to inform Members that the time for questions and comments has expired. Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald).

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity today to speak on Bill C-93, a long awaited Bill on multiculturalism. I suspect that this policy is something that all Canadians now approve of very heartily. Increasingly Canadians see that it is important to enshrine in legislation the policy we have had with us for a long time, the promotion of the cultural identity of people from all origins who make up Canada.
We think of the comparison with the United States where it has been said to be a melting pot. In Canada the late John Porter identified Canadian society as the vertical mosaic, that the different ethnic groups were part of Canada, they did not melt away in the melting pot as they did in the United States, but they were ranked, and some were more equal than others. Of course, that is unacceptable. What this Bill attempts to do, and what we all want to see done is to say that neither is right; we do not want a melting pot nor do we want the disappearance of the ethnic groups. We want the strength and richness in Canadian society of the contribution of different ethnic groups. However, we do not want ethnic groups to be ranked so that some people are below others or people from some
March 22, 1988

groups do not have the same chances as those from other groups. We want all Canadians to have equal rights. We want to see equality rights enshrined in the Bill.
I think the Bill addresses equality rights. All Canadians are equal and there ought not to be discrimination. We have nondiscrimination measures in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which are referred to in the Bill. Indeed we see that there are measures to strengthen them.
On the positive side we need to protect individual rights but also to promote the collective right, the survival of cultures. We need to do so because as it happens it makes us a better country and a better part of the world. It gives us links with other parts of the world if we maintain the different cultures.
My riding of Broadview-Greenwood is a well-known area. It is the heart of the Greek community of Toronto. It is a very desirable place in which to live. It is a very lively part of Toronto. We enjoy the opportunities to celebrate religious and national festivals. Indeed people who are not Greek Canadians join in these celebrations and find them to be a very attractive and important part of life in Toronto. We have a growing Chinese Canadian community. It is now attracting people of all communities to come there to shop, to enjoy restaurants, and so forth. It is developing in a very positive and desirable way as a part of Toronto.
We share the concerns of people who want to preserve the cultures which they bring with them to Canada. However, I must say that not everything is quite as rosy as we would like it to be. Discrimination still exists. There is discrimination on the basis of race against ethnic minorities who are visibly different. They experience more difficulties in obtaining jobs, keeping jobs, and getting promotions. We know about difficulties in policing and all kinds of difficulties which members of these groups experience.
The Bill does not go very far in this respect. There are other measures which try to deal with racism, but I should like to refer to a measure which is in Clause 5(g). It indicates that the Minister shall take such measures as he or she considers appropriate to implement the multiculturalism policy of Canada, specifically to "assist racial minority communities to conduct activities with a view to overcoming any discriminatory barrier". I note that it is not very high on the list and that it is fairly vague. It indicates that the Minister will help groups to overcome these barriers. It is a very modest step, but it is in the right direction. I welcome it, but I regret to say that much more is needed. We need to rely on the Canadian Human Rights Commission and the human rights commissions of the various provinces to defend victims of discrimination. In many cases they do not even get to the human rights commissions, because people must complain on an individual basis and they are afraid of retaliation. We still have a long way to go to make for improvements in this regard.
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
I should like to refer to an area in which I think some progress has been made. I am sure that anyone who supports Bill C-93 would be very glad about it. The Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, in its sixth report, contained proposals for a new Broadcasting Act and was very specific in recognizing multiculturalism. For example, recommendation No. 24 indicates what should be in the objectives part of the new Broadcasting Act. It says that the programming carried by the system should provide a balanced representation of Canadian society, reflecting its multicultural and bilingual realities, its aboriginal peoples, and the composition of its population in respect of sex, age, race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, and mental or physical handicap.
The message it gives is absolutely consistent with Bill C-93. It says that Canada is comprised of many different kinds of people and because broadcasting uses the public air waves it must reflect this diversity. It would be wrong for only one or two groups to dominate, to exclude, or to minimize the reflection of other groups by ethnicity and other criteria.
I think it is important. I hope the Government acts on it. If so, it will be for the first time that such a provision would actually be in the Broadcasting Act, and I think that the Broadcasting Act needs it.
There has been some improvement. CBC is showing greater diversity by using people of ethnic origin to do reporting and so forth. This is very healthy. It is realistic and it reflects Canada much more accurately. I welcome the steps which the CBC has taken. We have seen it as well in private stations.
Also the report on broadcasting recommended that appointments to the boards of the CRTC and the CBC should reflect ethnic diversity, going away from the vertical mosaic with British and French groups at the top and other groups underneath. Roughly a third of Canadians who come from groups other than the English and French ones ought to be well represented in official appointments. It is important that they be so represented in terms of broadcasting, and I think that it should be the case for all kinds of official appointments.
I hope the Government gives up its practice of patronage appointments and appointments on the basis of association with the Party in power and instead uses other criteria of merit.

Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Much more could be done. Multicultural groups have recommended-and the New Democratic Party has very actively supported them-a couple of specific measures which we think would be more effective than some of the measures in Bill C-93. One would be the proposal that the multicultural bureaucracy report to a full minister and deputy minister. In short, it is asking for a department of multiculturalism, not just a sub-department of some other ministry. This would give it higher status. Bureaucracies, ministers, and deputy ministers acquire their status through how much authority they have. It need not be a large department, but a separate department would say that we consider the matter important enough to have its own minister and deputy minister. I think that that would be a good move.
Another area in which I think there could be improvement would be to have a parliamentary commission on multiculturalism and a commissioner in charge who would report to Parliament. In short, the commissioner would report to all Parties and have some independence. The department or the sub-department, as the case may be, will of course report through its minister, through a political channel. If things do not go too well, they can be covered up through that kind of process. However, if we have an independent person, such as we have for official bilingualism, we would have a commissioner who would be in charge and would be a servant of Parliament. It would be a better and fairer structure. It would ensure that the watch-dog function is carried out properly. If the Government has nothing to hide, it ought to welcome this approach. We would ensure that its functions were properly carried out by ensuring that Parliament's own appointee is there.
Bill C-93 largely reflects policy that is already in existence. It begins with a very long preamble. This may or may not be a good thing. In fact, the preamble is practically longer than the Bill itself. It asserts very high-minded principles and refers to the Charter of Canada, the Constitution, the Official Languages Act, the Citizenship Act and all of these sorts of things. Of course, a preamble does not have any force of law and so much of this has to be reworded into the principles within the Bill itself. This Bill largely puts down on paper decisions that have been worked out over the last couple of decades which have very broad agreement across Canada and across all three political Parties.
Clause 3 declares it to be the policy of the Government of Canada to:
(a)	promote the understanding that multiculturalism reflects the cultural and racial diversity of Canadian society and acknowledges the freedom of all members of Canadian society to preserve and share their cultural heritage;
No one would disagree with that but it had not been stated in so many words before. We have just the beginning of recognition in the Constitution. This Bill flushes it out somewhat more when it states:
(b)	promote the understanding that multiculturalism is a basic element of the Canadian heritage ...
(c)	promote the full and equitable participation of individuals and communities of all origins in the continuing evolution and shaping of all aspects of Canadian society and assist them in the elimination of any barrier to such participation.
This is fairly vague language. They are high sounding principles which perhaps do not reflect the urgency that there is not this equality yet and that discrimination still exists. It is important that we reflect our concern with that ongoing discrimination and barriers which are not right. They are not what we want in our country. We want access for all people to find their own place in society and to make their own contribution. Clause 3(d) reads:
recognize the existence of communities whose members share a common origin and their historic contribution to Canadian society, and enhance their development;
I like this aspect of the Bill and this recognition that our concerns are not just with individual rights. Yes, there is a concern for individual rights and we must be vigilant and protect and enhance individual rights, but we must also ensure that communities be part of Canada. We are not a bunch of isolated atoms. We live in communities, and distinctive communities have their own contribution to make. I very much welcome this aspect of the Bill. I think it is important to our understanding of Canada as a community of communities.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

And then, showing this balance from communities to individuals, subparagraph (e) reads:
Ensure that all individuals receive equal treatment and equal protection under the law, while respecting and valuing their diversity.
There is a balancing act to be performed. Clause 3 has subparagraphs (a) through (j). Quite a number of these generalities reflect what is either existing practice or the policy and desire of Canadians to see that these matters be part of our Canadian society.
We might be a little critical at this stage and point out that these are vague and high sounding principles. So far there is nothing requiring action. The Minister is supposed to support these various things in some fashion or other. I think the criticisms which have been given by the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, for example, are quite germane. The Minister is not required to act. The Government is not required to do anything in particular to ensure that these objectives are actually put into practice. We get into another section of the Bill. Subclause (2) reads:
It is further declared to be the policy of the Government of Canada that all federal institutions should-
We go from the general policy to actual institutions, government boards, commissions, agencies and so forth. Again the paragraph talks about equal opportunity:
-to obtain employment and advancement in those institutions;
March 22, 1988

(b) promote policies, programs and practices that enhance the ability of individuals and communities of all origins to contribute to the continuing evolution of Canada.
We have the need, however, not just to talk about this in some vague fashion, but there are areas where we need to encourage it very specifically in hiring practices and training practices to see that the old barriers are changed. This is true for members of visible minorities, women, native people and the handicapped. We need particular programs to overcome the prejudice and discrimination of the past and the lack of experience because of that discrimination to see that those barriers really do go down and people have a chance to make their way and get some assistance in moving past those barriers that were erected and still exist. The wording of this statement is very vague. Unless there is government action by way of employment equity programs, of positive hiring practices to ensure that people in different groups hear about opportunities and have a chance to reply, to have their merits taken seriously, and unless there are particular ways of achieving it, it will just remain a high sounding principle and will not help anyone to overcome the barriers of the past. Subparagraph (c) reads:
Promote policies, programs and practices that enhance the understanding of and respect for the diversity of the members of Canadian society.
The broadcasting example I gave a few minutes ago is a practical example of what another committee is already doing with respect to the same principles. The Standing Committee on Communications and Culture is dealing with the broadcasting aspect. We are looking at advice to give to the Government for a new Broadcasting Act which we have not yet seen. We have been promised it for a long time and we rather expected it would be here. I hope we will see the Minister bring in a Bill that will enshrine that important symbolic area of broadcasting.
People spend a lot of time watching television and listening to radio. The images people see on the screen help to give them an idea of what Canada is all about. It is important that those institutions of broadcasting be honest and realistic in their reflection of Canadian reality, avoid negative stereotypes, show opportunities for people and show positive models for people to follow.
This will not just be words on paper that look great but do not mean anything in reality. It will require many institutions, if not all under a federal regulation, to act in their own particular way to see that multiculturalism is actually respected within their own framework.
In subparagraph (d) we read:
collect statistical data in order to enable the development of policies, programs and practices that are sensitive and responsive to the multicultural reality of Canada;
If we do not have the statistics, we do not know if we are making any progress. For people who have been discriminated against we need to see where they are in the system, at what level and what income gaps there are. We would like to see
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
clearly over time that those differences in income, salary, wages and so forth, percentages in different levels of our different federal agencies in the different jobs, are reduced over time. We know that talent exists in all these different groups. If people are not well distributed through the system, we have to suspect it is not lack of talent on the part of any particular group but perhaps lack of opportunity or some kind of either deliberate or inadvertent barrier. Clearly collecting appropriate statistics is important to see if we are actually making progress in being fairer to people.
The next subparagraph reads:
(e) make use, as appropriate, of the language skills and cultural understanding of individuals of all origins;
Let me briefly refer to this as I know I have to wind up. The language skills that people from many different cultural groups bring to Canada are important for Canada. We belong to the United Nations and to an international trading community. It is important that language skills be retained and developed so that Canada can play its part in the developing and in the trading world. These are assets which people bring to us from their own culture. We should be glad we have them and we should work actively to promote them.
Since my time is up, Mr. Speaker, let me say that I am pleased to take part in this debate to support the measures that are here already. The work is not over. We still need some other measures. I can assure you that my Party will be working to make these practicable, to see that they are realized and to see that we take the next steps the next time we work to improve and to ensure that we have a good statute on multiculturalism for Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I take great pride in rising in this House to add my voice in support of Bill C-93. I applaud the Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie), the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and all those who have worked with such diligence and devotion to prepare this legislation.
The message of this Bill is strong and clear. It affirms the multicultural and multiracial reality of our society. It affirms that cultural diversity enriches all Canadians. It affirms that our multicultural reality makes us more open and compassionate people while providing opportunities for our future prosperity in a global economy.
However, multiculturalism is more than a recognition of contemporary social realities. It is more than the retention of heritage, culture and languages, and it is more than freedom of

March 22, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
cultural expression and a fostering of equality. Multiculturalism is a dynamic force in our society which will not only propel us into the future but will also define what our future will be.
Multiculturalism is such a force because we recognize that it lies at the heart of our national identity, of our sense of being Canadian. Multiculturalism has meaning both for individuals and for the country as a whole. It is a way of creating a dynamic composite out of the many different elements which make up the Canadian way of life.
One of Canada's unique qualities has been an ability to build from diverse linguistic and cultural origins. Being Canadian means belonging to a united, bilingual, multicultural country. Being Canadian also means that 25 million people live in a free society which seeks constantly to adapt to changing social, economic and political realities, both at home and in the international sphere.
Bill C-93 is a vital part of that process, of the evolution of our nation. This Bill recognizes the strengths and benefits inherent in our pluralistic society. It recognizes our unique resources of skills, linguistic abilities and cultural knowledge which enrich our country at home and increase its international stature.
As Hon. Members are aware, the multiculturalism sector of the Department of Secretary of State administers a number of world-class programs designed to help retain the cultural richness inherent in our multicultural reality. These programs assist with research into cultural histories and fund theatre and the visual arts. They provide chairs of ethnic studies at many of our universities, and they generally help people give expression to their cultural values and ways of interpreting them. In so doing, of course, they also help to create a feeling of pride and self-worth.
Cultural retention, cultural pride and cultural communications are all essential ingredients if all Canadians are to achieve an active citizenship and a full involvement in this country. Fostering this spirit of active, involved citizenship is a major priority of this Government. It involves strengthening the sense of community that binds us together as a nation and it involves making our multicultural character understood and appreciated throughout Canada and the world.
Our record still needs improvement. We must continue to reduce the barriers to the full economic, social and political participation of all groups in our society. We want to educate Canadians on their own terms as to how a multicultural society contributes to a better life for us all.
It has been said that the best antidote to prejudice is education. That is why the Department of Secretary of State is promoting human rights education in the schools and the teaching of concepts of citizenship which include the recognition of multiculturalism in Canada. The need for this kind of education also produced the court challenges program administered by the Canadian Council for Social Development.
As Hon. Members are aware, this program supports challenges to the courts based on the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The aim is to help define how those freedoms apply in practice and to educate people about the nature of their rights.
Another government priority is a more complex and sensitive one. It involves changing attitudes to make people and institutions more sensitive to our multicultural reality and more responsive to its requirements.
Changing immigration patterns have greatly altered the demographic make-up of Canada. Census data from 1981 and 1986 show that the proportion of non-British and non-French groups has increased to the point where people with origins other than French or British represent over 37.5 per cent of the Canadian population. Collectively, these groups form the majority in Toronto and Vancouver and account for a significant proportion of Montreal's population.
More than one million Canadians are members of visible minority communities. Studies show that by the turn of the century, visible minorities will approach 10 per cent of the Canadian population. This trend presents new challenges for a society and its institutions. The challenge will be how to accept and interact with all cultural and racial groups so as to encourage their full participation as productive citizens.
The legislation proposed in Bill C-93 speaks to all Canadians, their communities and their institutions. It will give full legislative recognition to our cultural and racial diversity. However, because the Canadian Multiculturalism Act will accommodate the realities of tomorrow as well as today, it provides the basic elements of a race-relations strategy designed to encourage tolerance and understanding among all members of our society, now and in the future. This strategy will stress the need to promote public awareness, it will help combat racism and it will encourage institutions to adapt their policies and practices to ensure equality and accommodate racial and cultural differences.
As the custodian of many institutions, the federal Government will be challenged to provide leadership to ensure that discriminatory action or ways of thinking are discontinued and that federal institutions protect a vibrant image of Canada's cultural and racial diversity.
Bill C-93 will enhance Canadian citizenship. It will broaden the reach of Canada's two official languages and it will establish in law an affirmation of Canada's multicultural character. The Bill seeks to provide a legislative base, a statutory declaration of policy for what up until now has simply been a discretionary commitment by successive federal Governments.
As it now stands, the multicultural program could be either drastically reduced or fundamentally redirected, possibilities which worry many ethnocultural groups. A statute, on the other hand, will provide a specific vehicle for preserving and enhancing the multicultural heritage of Canadians as promised
March 22, 1988

in the Constitution. By officially recognizing the historic and future contributions of multiculturalism to Canadian society, the Bill will strengthen the sense of national unity among all Canadians and ethnocultural communities.
Perhaps an even greater asset of Bill C-93 is its determination in the pursuit of social justice. We as a nation have a long parliamentary commitment to social justice and human rights. Even before Confederation, Sir Hector Langevin declared that the Government should ensure justice to all races, to all religions, to all nationalities and to all interests. That was written in 1865. The far-sighted Sir Hector went on to become Canada's first Secretary of State.
Our approach to human rights and to a multiculturalism policy for Canada reinforce each other. The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in the 1982 constitutional Act is one of the strongest declarations of human rights anywhere in the world. These legal commitments are backed up by a strong judiciary, an active citizenship and a sensitive and responsive Government.
I believe that the multicultural nature of our society helped shape the kind of collective will which led to such a strong declaration of rights in our Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
That document guarantees rights for our aboriginal peoples, rights for the disabled, rights for women, rights for people of all races, colours and creeds in this country.
Multiculturalism is also a key element in Canada's profile abroad. Our determination to ensure cultural and racial equality provides a strong model for other plural societies, a model that has received international accolades.
I was pleased to learn that Sweden has indicated an interest to come to Canada to study and evaluate how our multicultural policy is working, with the hope of adapting a similar model in Sweden.
The image of Canada as a country that believes in cultural equality and human rights, and acts on what it believes, bolsters our credibility when we take a stand on international issues. It gives us a unique advantage in international diplomacy, especially on human rights issues.
Our commitment to multiculturalism as a force for change and growth within our society can have an impact on improved international relations. We have expertise and language abilities to tap in our culturally diverse society which can give us a unique advantage in world trade opportunities.
International trade is one means of binding together the world community. We become mutually dependent on each other and good social and political relations are almost inevitable outcomes of good economic relations.
Quite apart from using our multicultural expertise in the world community, we must nurture and safeguard the vast
Royal Assent
potential of multiculturalism within our own borders. This is an increasing realization that the future building of our nation will be dynamic and harmonious only to the extent to which it fully recognizes and includes all Canadians from every origin.
Bill C-93 acknowledges our respect for this country's racial and cultural diversity, and establishes our commitment to equality of access for every member of the Canadian family.
Our diversity is one of our greatest national assets. It has brought us enormous economic benefits and increasing international respect. It has attracted people to this country like a magnet from all corners of the globe.
Rather than diminishing our sense of a common identity, this collective diversity has enhanced our definition of being Canadian and has created an image of Canada as the world's first international nation.
This Government has clearly defined its vision of our Canadian identity as rooted in our citizenship values, our two official languages and our multicultural reality. Multiculturalism is a policy that promotes national unity and cultural harmony. It improves the quality of our daily life and offers important opportunities for the country's future prosperity.
Bill C-93 is based on these beliefs and on the conviction that all Canadians must have an equal chance to contribute to the dynamic multicultural evolution of our nation. By respecting the traditional diversity of our society and by looking to the future with a sure sense of the past, we have a stronger sense of ourselves. We know who we are and therefore we can better determine where we will go.
Bill C-93 is an affirmation of our Government's forwardlooking strategy. The passage into law of Bill C-93 will mark the start of a new era. Our children and grandchildren will look back on it as a symbol of our new maturity as a nation, a nation committed to fairness, equality and partnership among all Canadians.
