Mr. Speaker, I have a few questions for my colleague for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Witer), who stated he was very proud of the multiculturalism program in this country. He worked hard on the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism, which recommended that the Government introduce a multiculturalism Bill to strengthen multiculturalism as a national program.
The Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park, as a Government member, took part in the committee's work and added his name to the unanimous report.
I would therefore like to ask my colleague for Toronto, when he considers the reaction to our committee report, how does he feel about the many recommendations that were not accepted by the Government? Mr. Speaker, they are really significant in that they ensure the success of this policy on multiculturalism.
I respect the Hon. Member's word and I know he worked a lot on that committee. However, 1 would like him to answer this question and give this House his own view.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will know that we are now debating the principle of the Bill. I hope members of the standing committee will have an opportunity to examine this Bill carefully at committee stage and come back with recommendations to the House. The Hon. Member will know, as someone who has been close to this subject since as far back as the mid 1970s, that the progress we have seen in multiculturalism in this country has come in small steps. In multiculturalism, as in other areas of government, we do not achieve and accomplish everything we want in one day or one week.
The Member was present in Toronto at the hearings of the Committee on Multiculturalism and will know that the report to which he refers received a wide variety of reaction and opinion. There were those who thought that the report was right on. There were those who thought that the report went too far in making its recommendations. Of course, there were those who thought that it did not go far enough. Therefore, to suggest that there is unanimity in support among the ethnocultural communities on either the Bill before us or the report tabled by the standing committee would be inaccurate.
I hope that during the committee stage we will have the appropriate time to examine the existing legislation and perhaps improve it where required. However, and this is important to note, I have not heard anyone during this debate indicate that the introduction of this Bill is not a significant step in taking multiculturalism forward in Canada. It is to that aspect that I address my remarks today.

would be an opportunity to push a few more things through the window.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to confine myself to two minutes, albeit with some difficulty.
My colleague, the Member for York West (Mr. Marchi), asked an important question. He referred to two specific issues which are critical in any Bill. First, he said that the mere introduction of a Bill is not that significant. Mr. Speaker, I realize that there is only a short time before we receive Royal Assent, but I would like to say a few words on this very important Bill dealing with a very important subject.
I would ask the House to indulge me for a moment while I wallow a little bit in nostalgia. I grew up in the north end of Winnipeg, the society of which is a source of perhaps the majority of gag writers in Hollywood and senior bureaucrats in
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
Ottawa, which is a rare combination. It is certainly one of the parts of the country which combines the most interesting mixture of cultural groups; Ukrainians, Jews, Germans, Poles, even the odd Welsh Canadians, such as my family, which are in some ways the most ignored cultural minority in the country, aside from Liberals in western Canada.
I recall very vividly that one day in high school a good friend of mine by the name of Sawchuk came to school and announced that his name was no longer Sawchuk but was now Saunders. When we inquired as to why that was, he said that his father, who worked for one of Canada's largest department stores, had reached the point where he was looking for a promotion but that the condition of his promotion was that his name be changed.
At that age perhaps we did not have quite the same understanding of what that meant in terms of the indignity that was being imposed upon my friend and his family of having to deny their roots, their culture, their language, their heritage, and their history for the sake of getting a small promotion in one of Canada's largest companies.
I mention that, Mr. Speaker, because to me that is what the multicultural policy is all about. It is an attempt to respond to the second class citizenship which has been imposed on far too many Canadians. Simply because of what they are, not who they are, they are labelled, and because of name, language, or culture are stereotyped or type-cast and not given the same rights or recognition as are those who have had a longer history in this country or have the name of a French or English antecedent.
There is no doubt that we have made a lot of progress since then. There has been a lot of accomplishment, and even in this Chamber today we can see examples of Canadians who have come from non-French or English backgrounds who now exercise prominent roles of leadership in politics. The same is true in business, the arts, culture and professions throughout the country.
However, it would be wrong to say that we have reached a satisfactory state. I think we are a long way from that. We are, to my mind, as I understand it from my own community of Winnipeg, at a very important juncture. The sense of accomplishment and aspiration of a large majority of Canadians, about whom the Hon. Member from High Park was talking, is still restrained, still circumscribed by sometimes real discriminatory actions. I still think that is at the forefront of the multicultural issue.
There is the example of a young Vietnamese couple who came to this country when I was Minister of Immigration. Their children are about ready to enter university but do not have the money to go. It is simply an economic fact of life that they are not able to acquire the means to send their very bright and able kids to university. That is a form of discrimination.

March 22, 1988
Canadian Multiculturalism Act
The same thing we faced back in the 1940s and 1950s is there for that newer group.
I spoke to a Ukrainian business and professional group a few weeks ago. They have a great sense of still trying to search out their roots and language back in the Ukraine. They have a sense of denial. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), who is sitting opposite, knows of the problem of Ukrainians in the Soviet Union feeling that as a Government we must do more. I do not in any way take away from the efforts of the Secretary of State for External Affairs because he has made great efforts. But there is still a feeling of uncertainty, of a tentative acceptance. There is a feeling that they are still not fully, 100 per cent, guaranteed all their rights.
That is why, I think, my colleague, the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) has argued the need for a strengthened structure in this country, a more effective commissioner of multiculturalism, for example, to give strong, effective leadership in weaving that fabric together in a more effective way, of having in the federal apparatus individuals who, by way of their office, can provide further leadership.
A very important victory was won with Article 27 of the Charter which recognized the multicultural fact of Canada. It is important to note that recently a group of legal experts gathered together to determine the meaning of that article and said it is still an open question as to how it can be incorporated into the fabric of the rights of Canadians. We need someone to give initiative to this particular Bill to ensure that the right challenges are made in the courts and to ensure that Article 27 is given life and meaning.
Without that apparatus, without that ongoing watch-dog role, initiative role, I am afraid it will not happen. That is why the argument we are making is not against the principle of the Bill and not against the philosophy of the Bill. We are simply saying that it could be a lot more. The time and age calls for it. There is a certain kind of mustiness about the Bill. We are not going back to the time when one had to change one's name, but it is not the kind of Bill that will deal with the realities of today and, certainly, tomorrow.
The role of the federal Government, I believe, in this area, as in all areas of human rights, is to provide leadership, to show the way, not simply to follow. That is why the argument that we are making is that this Bill, as strong as it may be in philosophy, is weak in implementation and structure. It is weak in the real hard-nosed organizational ability which is required to make any bureaucracy or large organization work.
I will conclude my remarks because I know the royal presence is near and I do not want to frustrate that. We argue strongly that the Bill should be amended to take into account that leadership role in making the multicultural fact not just a philosophy but to bring it to its full fruition as a reality. That is why we hope government Members will be prepared to consider the kinds of amendments my colleague will bring forward.

Can the Chair clarify the procedure? Some Members are saying that I can ask a question of my colleague, although he has only completed five minutes of his 20-minute speech. Can we have a clarification on what is happening?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member has asked for clarification. The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod has not arrived. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) still has the floor.
Mr. Speaker, this is called "ragging the puck", is it?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is the only time we would encourage you to speak, Lloyd.

I thank the Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs for that warm endorsement.
As I was saying, one of the reasons for this kind of Bill is to give that leadership. Let me point to another example that triggered my interest when the Member from High Park was speaking. I believe he touched upon a very important aspect of multiculturalism, one that has not been properly developed, that is, the utilization of part of its characteristics, as a way of extending ourselves to the rest of the world. I do not think there is any argument that we live in a time when all of us must realize we are going to have to be much more competitive and effective in terms of our international economic and political relations.
I was struck again by that thought three or four months ago when I was at a hearing in Edmonton. A coalition of ethnic leaders appeared before our trade task force and pointed out that very limited development takes place in terms of the use of our cultural heritage for trade promotion or development in terms of learning other languages, learning about other cultures and using the strengths so many of these groups bring to our country. We are not properly exploiting them. 1 address this point to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He knows I have other grievances about the cut-backs on promotion and development work.
It would seem to me that a very major role would be to utilize, through our universities, colleges and schools, the kind of strength that can arise out of this emergence of multiculturalism. Let us talk about the Pacific Rim, for instance. There is an incredible richness of the Indo-Chinese population in Canada in terms of opening up avenues of understanding for the rest of Canadians.
We can also use that as a ways of developing our opportunities abroad. That seems to me one of the aspects of multiculturalism I have talked about, the new fabric or new reality. These people are saying: "We are here. We have skills. We have now reached a point in our own maturity. Use us. Put us to work". But we need some support in doing that. I do not have a perfectly calculated formula but, I think the objective is worthy. I think what should be looked at is how the federal Government can work out the proper means and mechanisms.
March 22, 1988

That comes back to the basic thesis we have followed in this debate.
We do not believe this Bill enables us to do that. We do not believe there is sufficient presence of the multicultural fact in the federal Government, either at the ministerial or departmental level or at the commissioner level, to give us the capacity to wield our influence and to bring about those kinds of judgment calls that are required.
There are two very different areas, one is the case of the prosecution of Article 27 of the Charter, extending it over to basic economic fact in the area of trade. There are two ways in which we could substantially exploit and develop the new reality of Canada, something we have not done. We ask, why not? Part of the reason has been the way the multicultural issue has got stuck in a time warp at the federal level. I think this legislation is partly a reflection of that. We have become perhaps too used to the conventional ways of doing things and we have not attempted to go beyond those things. We have not opened up our opportunity for further development in this area.
Let me point to yet another area where I think we must develop the multicultural fact where federal leadership will be required, that is, on the side of immigration that does not deal with people coming to this country. It is what happens when people get here. There has been a long-standing argument and debate between federal bureaucracies, between the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Employment and Immigration, about their role in the settlement and development of immigrants once they arrive, to say nothing about the debate between the provinces and the federal Government. That is still a debate that is unresolved. It has still not been given the kind of clear direction it requires. Yet we see all kinds of examples, whether it is in the area of the development of language skills for immigrant women or whether it is with respect to training skills for people who are in the refugee stream. In these areas it is still somewhat of a patchwork arrangement.
Once again, it seems to me that if there were somebody, both in terms of a department with a clear interest or even a commissioner of multiculturalism, then that would be a cause that they could take up. They could provide the focal point within this type of vast apparatus around Ottawa to try to bring it all together and to get the factions and the departments which are each fighting for their turf to say, "Wait a minute. There is a very important issue happening here".
Once again, I do not see it happening. Part of the reason is the vacuum. That role is not being exercised as it effectively should be exercised.
I offer that comment as a demonstration of the case made by my colleague about the need not only to think forward but to have the means and organizational strength at the federal level to do so.
Royal Assent
I also bring up this point concerning the area in which we relate to other jurisdictions, particularly to the provinces but to the municipalities as well. I do not have the latest account, but I have been intrigued by the number of cities which have had to set up race relations commissions. In Toronto and in my own city of Winnipeg this has been done. These commissions play very important roles because they are dealing right at the ground level with problems of discrimination in hiring practices. In some cases they are dealing with actual conflicts between different cultural or racial groups.
There was an example just recently in the case of police relations with cultural groups. This is something which is becoming far too common, unfortunately so, in our cities. The question I asked and one which I pose again to members of the Cabinet is this one. Who is responsible at the federal level for relating to that real issue that is taking place in Vancouver, Toronto and Winnipeg? Who is working with those very important grass-root racial commissions to see what might be done to try to co-ordinate, whether it is employment programs or the immigrant development programs about which I spoke?
There may be individual Members of Parliament doing it. But they do it in a piecemeal fashion. Some may go to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard). As I recall, the commission in Toronto came to me when I held that post to say that there was an emergence up in the York area of some real gang problems with young visible minorities. Kids were running into real problems and conflict on the streets. I was asked if I could help with a couple of employment programs in that area.
That was but one piece of the puzzle. The problem is, who do we go to at the federal level to organize the entire issue for us all? I do not think there is that person there right now.
I use those examples simply by way of argument to show why it is important that this Bill be strengthened substantially and that the proper and useful principle that it espouses be given a much more effective form or structure by the time we debate this Bill at third reading.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PARLIAMENT HILL PROPOSED ERECTION OF STATUE OF QUEEN ELIZABETH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to add a few remarks today to the remarks of many of my colleagues in the House from all three Parties concerning the motion in the name of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Tupper) that a statue be erected to commemorate the contribution of Her Majesty, Queen Elizabeth II, to Canadian society.
The suggestion made by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) that a commission be established to look into the number and nature of statues to be erected on Parliament Hill is a good one and worth following.
Most of us in the House have lived most of our lives in the reign of Queen Elizabeth II. The contributions of this monarch
have been very considerable to Canadian society, to the society of the Commonwealth, and to the society of Great Britain where she customarily has her residence. The parallel has been drawn between Queen Elizabeth II and Queen Victoria. Those two monarchs have reigned in Canada for 100 of the last 161 years. That reflects the contribution of two great women, according to the lights of their own belief and the values of their own time, to the development of Canadian society and indeed to the development of the Commonwealth as a whole.
The ascension of Queen Elizabeth II to the Throne is a day that is very fresh in my memory. Her father, the late King George VI, died on my sixth birthday. Thus, since my sixth birthday, both in Great Britain and here in Canada, I have only known Queen Elizabeth II as the reigning monarch. Therefore, I think it fair to say that my formative years, my maturing years, and the years of my adulthood and political career have been spent under the reign of Queen Elizabeth II.
She has surely seen some changes in those 36 years. After all, in 1952 when she acceded to the Throne, the Commonwealth was by and large made up of colonies which were in some form of tutelage or subordinate relationship to Great Britain under the British Crown.
Now I believe that we can truly say that the Commonwealth is a commonwealth of nations where all, despite differences in size, prosperity, and influence within world society, are rightly and correctly treated as being equal within the framework of the Commonwealth.
The Commonwealth has not been an institution merely for the preservation, the spread, or even the development of British culture. It has become a forum where nations that share a common heritage, particularly in terms of their institutions as well as the English language, can discuss matters of world affairs and can, when the spirit moves them, exercise collective influence on those world affairs.
Having set the historical context, and turning to the matter of the statue, it seems to me that one of the practicalities in such an initiative would be to ask Her Majesty if she would like to see a statue erected on Parliament Hill within her lifetime. It has not been the practice in Britain, although it is in some countries, to erect statues during the lifetime of the person commemorated or represented by the statue. It is still not something about which many of us who have British heritage feel particularly comfortable.
Many excellent suggestions have been made in this debate concerning other people who might be commemorated. I do not feel it demeans or derogates in any way from Her Majesty the Queen and Her achievements to discuss that in the context of this motion. After all, the opportunity to discuss such a topic, important and interesting as it is, does not come regularly or frequently to us by way of any other opportunity. This is not to establish any form of comparison between Her Majesty and other people who might be commemorated, but to suggest that not only the political history, political traditions, and political life of Canada should be commemorated by way
March 22, 1988

of statues on Parliament Hill, but many other integral and fundamental Canadian values, Canadian activities, and Canadian achievements should also be considered in the erection of statues.
Because we are an extremely far-flung federal nation, we should consider whether we should concentrate our efforts, energies, and attention on the statues which should be erected on Parliament Hill or whether we should set our scopes wider and look at other strategic or historic locations where statues might be erected.
Of course the matter of partisanship must always be avoided in the consideration of the erection of statues. It does not come into the consideration of the present motion since the Queen and the institution of the monarchy historically, and certainly
Statue of Monarch
today, have been above the level of political partisanship and political fray.
